articles.title: Trump's promise of 300,000 tons of tariff-reduced beef imports to reduce grocery costs falls short - Fortune
articles.summary: Trump's promise of 300,000 tons of tariff-reduced beef imports to reduce grocery costs falls short  FortuneTrump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports  Al JazeeraTrump’s Plan to Import More Ground Beef Is Falling Short  The New York TimesExperts: Beef is Enjoying a Moment Culturally and Economically, but Questions Loom Large on Horizon  Arkansas Money & PoliticsDemocrats woo farmers on beef with President Donald Trump &...
articles.full_text:
At the nexus of an ongoing affordability crisis and midterm election push, the Trump administration’s effort to reduce beef prices appears to be falling short.
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation in August to temporarily increase the quantity of beef in the U.S. by importing 300,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings into the country at a reduced tariff rate. The imports were scheduled over 90 days, from September through November.
“This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again,” Trump wrote on Truth Social announcing the policy.
But as of Oct. 19, the U.S. has imported just 59,423 metric tons of beef, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data, or just 20% of the target. And ground beef averaged $6.79 per pound as of September, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, down from $6.92 in August, but still above $6.32 a year ago.
This 7% year-over-year increase in beef, due to persistently high demand as well as dwindling herd sizes, has far outpaced the 2.5%-2.9% hike in overall U.S. grocery prices, which has become representative of America’s affordability woes. Trump has identified beef prices as a key issue to address during the second half of his term, as he targets policy toward the typically loyal Republican base of farmers.
“It really became unacceptable to the voter,” Trump said last month. “And we do have to get elected, because if we’re not going to get elected, your ranchers and your farmers are in big trouble.”
But both farmers and agricultural economists are doubtful that 300,000 tons of imported beef will deliver price cuts, arguing the initiative is ineffective at best, and a financial strain during an already challenging period for the industry at worst.
“The simple assumption there was that if we can just increase supply of beef in the U.S., that should lower prices,” Derrell Peel, a professor of agribusiness specializing in livestock at Oklahoma State University, told Fortune. “Unfortunately, the beef industry is much more complex than that.”
The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.
Why Trump’s push for lower beef costs are falling short
Part of why Americans aren’t seeing a noticeable difference in beef costs is because the type of beef being sent from overseas doesn’t typically hit retail shelves, Peel noted. Lean beef trimmings are often combined with fatty trimmings produced from cattle in American feed lots. This combination of beef is usually used by fast food restaurants, not grocery stores where many American consumers are looking for relief.
The use of these lean trimmings as a complement to domestic fatty trimmings also means the demand for this type of beef is already modulated. The beef industry is able to import lean trimmings to meet demand, even absorbing tariffs to do so, according to Peel, and therefore an influx of supply at a cheaper cost doesn’t address the underlying retail cost issue.
“When you take away the tariff, you make it cheaper, but you don’t necessarily increase the demand because we only need so much of it,” Peel said. “We were getting as much as we wanted.”
In addition, Brazil and Argentina, which account for much of America’s imported beef, have their own supply issues with low beef inventory.
Glynn Tonsor, an agricultural economics professor at Kansas State University, argued that if Trump wanted to truly lower beef prices, the best way to do so would be to not interfere with the prices to begin with, allowing them to rise.
“If you erode beef demand, you will erode beef prices,” he told Fortune.
Beef demand has stayed high even as prices have soared, increasing 5.9% in the first six months of 2026 compared to the same period a year before. Tonsor blames demand, not smaller cattle herds, for higher prices. Herd sizes have been on the decline for 60 years, he noted, making them a predictable factor for the industry and therefore only partly responsible for more expensive beef.
If prices remain high, it will effectively destroy demand and eventually ease prices. But that would also slow imports, not increase them, Tonsor said, meaning there would be no need or reasonable expectation for 300,000 metric tons of beef to enter the country.
American farmers’ beef with Trump
Farmers are largely uninterested in an intervention that would lower beef prices. American Farm Bureau Federation President Zippy Duvall asked Trump to roll back the policy in a statement last month, arguing the imports would lower cattle prices and could cost ranchers $300 to $400 per head.
“To put it simply, the plan undercut a fragile recovery in the cattle industry while failing to benefit consumers,” Duvall said.
What’s preventing farmers from being more upset about Trump’s import policy is its lack of efficacy, Peel noted. If there were more imports, cattle prices would be depressed, but the modest uptick has not had an overwhelming impact on the industry.
Instead, farmers are most upset about the president’s interference in an industry that has historically favored a free market, Peel explained.
“Nothing is simple here,” he said. “There’s no simple answer when it comes to anything you might want to do policy-wise to influence this market.”

articles.title: USTR weighs extending pause on China-linked vessel fees to January - Supply Chain Dive
articles.summary: USTR weighs extending pause on China-linked vessel fees to January  Supply Chain Dive
articles.full_text:
The Office of the United States Trade Representative is proposing to extend its suspension on Section 301 fees on China-linked vessels until Jan. 9, 2027, according to an Oct. 23 Federal Register filing. The suspension is currently set to lift on Nov. 9.
The proposed extension would “allow for further negotiation with China regarding the acts, policies, and practices at issue in this investigation,” per the federal filing. Comments are being fielded from the public, which are due on Oct. 30.
Last year, the USTR announced fees ranging from $18 per ton to $120 per container due to China’s role in the logistics, maritime and shipbuilding sectors. The policy aimed to incentivize domestic shipbuilding by offering vessel owners an up-to-three-year exemption on fees if they ordered a new U.S.-built vessel. Proposed fees were set to start on Oct. 14 of last year but were first paused until November 2025. A year later, stakeholders are still wary of the fees.
Last month, several trade groups and shipper assocations urged U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to extend the exisitng pause on Section 301 vessel fees. In a letter, stakeholders expressed concern that the fees could further ocean freight market uncertainty, which is facing elevated transportation costs and shifting carrier capacity.
“[I]mposing new or resumed fees on China-built or China-linked vessels would create immediate and far-reaching consequences for U.S. companies that rely on ocean transportation to move goods into and out of the United States,” stakeholders wrote in the letter to Greer.

articles.title: India's textile industry targets USD 350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound: Report - Big News Network.com
articles.summary: India's textile industry targets USD 350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound: Report  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
New Delhi [India], October 26 (ANI): India's textile industry expanded to nearly USD 190 billion in FY26 and now targets USD 350 billion by 2030, driven by domestic demand, manufacturing investments, and export opportunities, according to the latest report by Rubix Data Sciences.
The report noted that the sector remains a primary employment generator while the central government considers a Rs 400 billion, five-year Textile Expansion and Employment (TEEM) Scheme to upgrade machinery, deploy advanced technology, and modernise traditional clusters.
The expansion comes as outbound shipments rebound. Textile exports, including handicrafts, grew by 10.3 per cent year-on-year in the April-August 2026 period. The recovery follows a 2.7 per cent decline to USD 35.8 billion in FY2026, even as imports climbed 17.1 per cent to USD 9.6 billion.
Despite the divergence, India maintained a net exporter position, with total outbound shipments standing at nearly 3.7 times the value of inbound shipments. Readymade garments retained a 44 per cent share of exports, while man-made fibre textiles accounted for 15 per cent.
Tushar Bhaskar, President of Rubix Data Sciences, noted that the sector continues to navigate external headwinds alongside domestic growth.
"India's textile industry has shown resilience, with exports growing 10.3% in April-August 2026 after a 2.7% decline in Dollar terms in FY2026," Bhaskar said.
"At the same time, trade uncertainty in the US market, a rise of approximately 60% in cotton yarn prices, and freight disruptions are adding to the pressure," he added. "This reinforces the importance of diversifying India's export destinations and improving cost competitiveness."
According to the report, the United States remained India's largest destination, taking 31 per cent of shipments in FY2026, followed by the European Union at nearly 16 per cent. However, trade dynamics shifted after the US introduced an additional 10 per cent duty under Section 301 measures in July 2026 concerning forced-labour enforcement, while broader negotiations stalled.
In response, domestic manufacturers accelerated market diversification. Shipments to the US fell approximately 7 per cent in FY2026, while deliveries to major European markets grew 9 per cent. Raymond Lifestyle plans to reduce its US export share from 65 per cent to between 55 and 60 per cent within two years, while Kitex Garments plans to lower its exposure from nearly 100 per cent to between 30 and 35 per cent over the next two to three years.
Input cost inflation also affected the domestic value chain. Cotton yarn prices climbed roughly 60 per cent to Rs 400 per kilogram in September 2026 from Rs 250 per kilogram in early 2026. The increase coincided with local cotton production dropping to 290.91 lakh bales in the 2025-26 season, down from 352.48 lakh bales in 2020-21. To assist mills, authorities granted an exemption on the 11 per cent cotton import duty through October 31, 2026.
Industrial infrastructure activity provided capital momentum. Investment proposals under the seven approved PM Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel Parks reached Rs 685.9 billion by August 2026, led by major expansion outlays from corporate producers including Grasim Industries and Vardhman Textiles. (ANI)

articles.title: Chinese automakers expand manufacturing in Europe to avoid EU tariffs amid rising domestic competition: Repo.. - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Chinese automakers expand manufacturing in Europe to avoid EU tariffs amid rising domestic competition: Repo..  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Chinese automotive giants, such as BYD and Geely, are setting up production plants in Europe. This strategic initiative helps them sidestep steep EU import taxes on electric vehicles, significantly lowering costs. By investing more in local manufacturing, they cultivate better connections with European suppliers, boosting operational efficiency.
According to the report, Chinese automakers, including BYD, Chery and Geely, are shifting production closer to European markets amid intense domestic competition and excess manufacturing capacity. Beyond avoiding European Union (EU) tariffs, these companies are leveraging underutilised factories and local partnerships to establish a long-term presence in Europe's automotive industry.
"The expansion marks a new phase in China's global automotive ambitions, testing whether its advantages in cost, scale and electric vehicle technology can be replicated overseas," the report said.
At the same time, it noted, for Hyundai Motor Group, which has spent decades building a European manufacturing network, the transformation brings a "formidable new challenge" as Chinese rivals increasingly compete on its turf.
Hence, local production offers a significant advantage in navigating EU trade restrictions, it noted.
Chinese-made battery electric vehicles (EVs) are subject to a standard 10 per cent import duty in the European Union (EU), along with additional countervailing tariffs ranging from 7.8 per cent to 35.3 per cent, depending on the manufacturer.
BYD faces an additional tariff of 17 per cent, while Geely and SAIC Motor face levies of 18.8 per cent and 35.3 per cent, respectively.
Thus, setting up manufacturing facilities within the EU would enable Chinese automakers to avoid these additional import tariffs, lower shipping costs and strengthen ties with local suppliers.
Notably, other Chinese manufacturers are pursuing similar strategies. SAIC Motor, which sells vehicles primarily under its MG brand, has explored plans for a European production facility as it seeks to reduce reliance on imports from China, the report said.
Additionally, "Chinese automakers are increasingly forming alliances with established manufacturers that are struggling with sluggish demand, costly electrification investments and underused production capacity."
It should also be noted that Chinese brands' European sales jumped 90.6 per cent year-on-year to 531,862 vehicles in the first half of 2026, The Korea Herald reported, citing market research firm MarkLines.
"Chinese manufacturers are expanding beyond battery-electric vehicles into plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids," it noted.
While this shift may help the struggling European factories stay open, it also raises questions about the region's growing reliance on China.

Coffee prices today, October 26, 2026
 World coffee prices have been trending negatively this past week.
 The coffee market plummeted this week as new crop supply put pressure on the market. On the London exchange, robusta coffee futures for November 2026 delivery closed the week at $3,228 per ton, a sharp decrease of 5.4% ($186 per ton) compared to the previous week. The January 2027 contract fell 4.8% ($163 per ton), reaching $3,242 per ton.
 On the New York Stock Exchange, the price of Arabica coffee for December 2026 delivery rose slightly by 0.6% (1.8 US cents/pound), reaching 307.45 US cents/pound. Conversely, the March 2027 contract fell by 0.4% (1.1 US cents/pound), to 293.40 US cents/pound. Further delivery contracts also saw declines ranging from 2.75 to 4.05 cents/lb.
 Robusta coffee prices are under downward pressure amid increased selling activity in Brazil and the prospect of new supply from the Vietnamese harvest. Data released by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) shows that in the week ending October 20th, speculators on the ICE exchange shifted from a net short position in arabica coffee to a net long position of 2,744 contracts.
 Conversely, Arabica coffee prices continue to be supported by limited supply and low inventory levels on the ICE exchange. Robusta prices, on the other hand, are under downward pressure due to increased selling activity in Brazil and the prospect of new supply from the upcoming harvest in Vietnam.
 According to the USDA, in the 2026-2027 crop year, replanted or newly planted coffee areas will enter a stable harvesting phase, with the potential for high yields. In addition, high coffee prices in the 2024-2025 crop year encouraged expansion of coffee cultivation, with large private enterprises increasing their scale of operations.
 In May, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) projected that Vietnam's coffee production in the 2026-2027 crop year would increase by 2.5% compared to the previous year, reaching 32.5 million bags (60 kg/bag). Of this, robusta production is expected to increase by 3%, to 31.4 million bags.
 Meanwhile, the Center for Advanced Studies in Applied Economics (Cepea), affiliated with the University of São Paulo, reported that Brazil concluded the first quarter of the 2026-2027 coffee crop year with the second-highest export volume ever recorded for the same period.
 According to data from the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association (Cecafé), total exports, including green coffee, roasted coffee, and instant coffee, reached 11.2 million 60-kg bags between July and September. This represents a 15.5% increase compared to the 9.7 million bags exported during the same period of the 2025-2026 crop year, second only to the record 12.2 million bags recorded in the first quarter of the 2024-2025 crop year.
 The USDA forecasts Brazil's coffee exports to reach a record 49.1 million bags in the 2026-2027 crop year, requiring Brazil to export approximately 37.9 million bags in the remaining nine months of the crop year.
 Assessing future market trends, industry experts believe that this price drop is a technical correction after a period of rapid growth, influenced by profit-taking pressure from international investment funds and signs of improved supply in some major exporting countries.
 Currently, the abundant supply of newly harvested coffee, coupled with strong international demand, has helped maintain sales momentum. The market is now focusing on the upcoming harvest in Vietnam, a factor expected to influence export activity in the coming months.
 However, in the longer term, attention is now shifting to the 2027-2028 crop year. Industry experts are increasingly concerned about the impact of El Niño, although they warn that it is still too early to assess the extent of the effect. El Niño is predicted to be very severe and could affect yields in the 2027-2028 crop year. Water resources for irrigation are also projected to be insufficient.
 Domestic coffee prices fell sharply last week, dropping by 3,100-3,500 VND/kg to below 90,000 VND/kg. 
 Domestic coffee prices have fallen across the board, following the weakening trend in the global market, with the lowest price recorded at 89,000 VND. This decline in domestic coffee prices stems directly from negative fluctuations on the two major international coffee exchanges, London and New York.
 Domestic trading activity remains relatively quiet, as traders await new coffee supplies from the current harvest. Traders report that trading activity is still subdued. Some exporters have begun exploring prices, but no agreements have been signed yet.
 The Vietnam Coffee Association (VICOFA) announced this week that the country's coffee production for the 2025-2026 crop year is estimated at nearly 1.9 million tons, a 6-10% increase compared to the previous crop year. However, traders and market participants forecast that the current crop year's production will generally remain largely unchanged compared to the 2025-2026 crop year.
 Weather conditions this year have been quite erratic in the Central Highlands, Vietnam's main coffee-growing region. Decreased yields in some areas have been offset by increased production in others. Newly planted coffee trees in some regions are yielding higher productivity, helping to compensate for the decline in output.
 In the short term, the domestic market is expected to remain cautious, closely monitoring developments on global markets in the following trading sessions as market participants await further information on global harvest and inventory levels. Cooperatives and individual producers need to continue closely monitoring market developments to develop flexible consumption and storage strategies, mitigating risks from unpredictable fluctuations in global agricultural prices.

articles.title: Can the courts end Trump's illegal tariffs? - Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.summary: Can the courts end Trump's illegal tariffs?  Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.full_text:
There was rejoicing in the anti-tariff world, including among American consumers and businesses relying on imported inputs on February 20, when the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs of 10 percent or higher that President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
That said, the basic 10 percent blanket tariff stayed in place as if nothing had happened. The president invoked another tariff statute, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, for, the president said, balance of payments reasons. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a division of the Department of Homeland Security, immediately imposed this new tariff taking effect simultaneously with the end of the now illegal IEEPA tariff. That made the IEEPA victory seem somewhat hollow. Yes, there would be refunds, billions of dollars of them, but the new 10 percent tariff stayed in place.
This second blanket tariff, for supposed balance of payments reasons under Section 122, was declared illegal by the Court of International Trade on May 7. But as the balance of payments authority is limited to 150 days, when it expired on July 24 the administration was ready yet again with a new basis for a presidentially imposed blanket tariff.
The US Trade Representative (USTR), using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, declared retaliation immediately against almost all exporting countries, which account for almost all of US trade, on the ground that these trading partners engaged in acts, policies, or practices that burden US commerce. How did so many countries merit this treatment? They were found by USTR to have fallen short of a newly-created standard none could meet: the vigor with which they could and did act against imports of goods into their own countries that might have been tainted by the use of forced labor. USTR's retaliatory "forced labor" tariffs were set again at a rate of at least 10 percent and took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on July 24, 2026, seamlessly, at the same moment that the balance of payments tariff ended.
That latest blanket tariff is still in place. The challenge to its legality is under consideration by the Court of International Trade, with a ruling expected any day.
Why haven't the courts been more effectual in eliminating the tariffs?
First, the administration has been skillful at shifting the basis for its presidential fiat tariff, pivoting from a nonexistent emergency to a nonexistent balance of payments problem to a supposed need for retaliation for an alleged unfair trade practice. There was no precedent for blanket tariffs imposed by presidential fiat in the 250-year history of the country until the second Trump administration took office.
The courts are a co-equal branch of government along with the executive and legislative. Each operates within constraints. The constraints on the Congress are plain to see. The Republican majority does not question this president's acts. The minority may be opposed but it has no effect. The Supreme Court has immunized the president against responsibility, either civil or criminal, for his acts done in the name of official business. He appears to be unconstrained, including by norms, the practices of all prior presidents.
There are certain basic constraints on the courts. There must be a case or controversy (Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 of the US Constitution). The courts cannot take issue with a policy judges do not like absent a case coming before them. But once a court has taken a case, it has wide latitude as to what it will decide, subject only to the norms it usually follows on how courts usually approach a solution. Could the courts have been more effective?
The Supreme Court could have struck down the emergency (IEEPA) tariffs as an unconstitutional invasion of Congress's prerogatives. Instead, perhaps to obtain a basis on which a majority of the justices could agree, it chose to rule against the emergency tariff on a technical reading of the text of the statute, arguing that it did not authorize the use of tariffs. This, however opened a door for the administration to try again to usurp Congress's power to tax.
The legitimacy of the five-month Section 122 balance of payments tariff is now being litigated on appeal. The Court of International Trade, a specialized court established by Congress, refrained from declaring that second tariff power grab unconstitutional. Rather it delved into the mysteries of the nation's international monetary accounts and determined that the statutory tests of what constituted a "balance of payments problem" were not met.
This is what courts do. They do not lightly find constitutional questions to resolve but see if the text of the statute itself serves as a basis for declaring a presidential action illegal, as being ultra vires, beyond the president's powers.
I assume the president will ultimately lose his Section 301 forced labor case, Burlap and Barrel, Inc. v. United States, No. 1:26-cv-03345. I have joined with two other veterans of the Office of the US Trade Representative—former USTR Carla Hills and former USTR General Counsel and White House official Warren Maruyama—to file an amicus brief in the current court case, taking the side of the small importers. We argue that Section 301 is only for use against individual countries' practices, not a global measure like Section 122. We state that no prior administration and no Congress in its drafting of the provision, or subsequently in is amendments of the statute, ever indicated that Section 301 conferred global tariff authority. We argue that Section 301 could not do so under the Constitution and that USTR's forced labor Section 301 cases were arbitrary and capricious, and not authorized by law.
Oral argument was held on September 30 before a three-judge panel of the Court of International Trade (CIT). The two-and-a-half hours of questions from the judges did not address the constitutionality of the forced labor tariff. The judges seemed unwilling to question whether the purpose of bundling 60 notionally separate Section 301 investigations was spurious in its entirety or that USTR was motivated primarily by a desire to deliver for the president a continuation of his invalidated broad tariffs. Rather, the CIT judges focused on the definitions that the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-418) added to Section 301 and expressed surprise that the administration had not investigated provisions that specifically referred to forced labor. We did not address that Section 301 language in our amicus brief. Indeed, the assistant attorney general arguing the case for the government admitted that USTR did not see this language as particularly relevant. That admission could undermine USTR's use of Section 301 to punish countries over dealing with foreign forced labor practices affecting their own imports.
Whether the CIT could remand the case back to USTR to address any shortcomings of its investigation is not clear. If the court does rule against the government, an appeal is likely, during which the court is unlikely to enjoin collection of tariffs, which has not been considered irremediable harm justifying an injunction.
If the administration loses the forced labor cases, the result will not be the complete elimination of tariffs imposed by this president and his executive branch. Pending are 16 "excess capacity" Section 301 cases1 and that is just a current example; other Section 301 cases can be formulated. Tariffs will not be eliminated until a court, and ultimately the Supreme Court, states that the fundamental issue is that under the Constitution, it is solely the Congress that has the power to tax; it cannot be delegated to the extent that the president sets the tariff of the United States in its entirety or anything approaching that, which he did with IEEPA, with the balance of payments authority, and by bringing multiple claims of unfair trade practices against the United States' more important trading partners.
What we have seen to date is that the executive branch, with its ability to move instantly, has been able to find the means to impose tariffs far faster than the courts can review their legitimacy.
The fundamental question is whether any court, and perhaps finally the Supreme Court, will choose to use the forced labor Section 301 case to bring to an end to Trump's serial attempts to illegally usurp the Congress's power over tariffs. Findings that statutes were misapplied or investigations were inadequate—the normal outcomes in judicial review of executive branch actions—are not enough. No matter how many cases the administration loses, tariffs will likely remain in place for the duration of the Trump administration, absent a finding that there is no broad tariff authority delegated to the president nor can there be.
The court under Chief Justice John Roberts has repeatedly reached for a sweeping result when a majority sees that doing so is warranted. It did so by ending judicial deference to executive agencies' interpretation of their own authority (ending the Chevron doctrine, Loper Bright v. Raimondo) as opposed to deferring to the office of the president.
The challenge to the Section 301 forced labor tariff case is an opportune time and place for the Supreme Court to defend the constitutional division of powers over imposing tariffs. Whether it will do so is far from guaranteed, but there is no evidence that Trump will cease imposing whatever broad tariffs he wishes independently of Congress until it does so.

articles.title: Why does the Ministry of Industry and Trade want to immediately implement the five-tiered electricity pricing system? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Why does the Ministry of Industry and Trade want to immediately implement the five-tiered electricity pricing system?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - The Ministry of Industry and Trade wants to immediately implement the five-tiered electricity pricing system to resolve issues regarding the implementation timeline, meet voter recommendations, and put the issued policy into practice.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade is seeking feedback on a draft Decision amending and supplementing several articles of Decision 14/2025 on the structure of retail electricity tariffs. A notable point is the proposal to remove the regulation requiring users to wait until the next adjustment of the average retail electricity price before applying the new tariff structure.
According to the drafting agency, if the draft is approved, the new retail electricity pricing structure, including a five-tiered residential electricity tariff and new peak and off-peak hours for manufacturing and business customers, will be applied immediately upon the amendment taking effect.
Why do they want to implement it immediately, without waiting for electricity price adjustments?
According to the submission, Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, issued on May 29, 2025, stipulates a new retail electricity pricing structure. However, this decision stipulates that the new pricing structure will only be applied from the date of the most recent adjustment of the average retail electricity price following the effective date of the document.
Since there has been no adjustment to the average retail electricity price since then, the new tariff structure has not yet been implemented in practice. The current electricity price continues to be applied according to the structure stipulated in Decision 28/2014/QĐ-TTg.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade believes that the regulations on the implementation timing need to be amended to resolve this issue, putting the new tariff structure into practice as soon as the amendment decision takes effect, regardless of when the average electricity price is adjusted.
One of the reasons cited by the Ministry of Industry and Trade is the recommendation from the Committee on Citizen Petitions and Supervision regarding the early implementation of the new electricity tariff.
According to the submission, in Report 1496/BC-UBDNGS16 dated October 1st sent to the Standing Committee of the National Assembly on the results of monitoring the resolution and response to voters' petitions, this agency requested the Ministry of Industry and Trade to urgently develop and submit to the Prime Minister for promulgation a decision amending and supplementing Decision 14/2025/QĐ-TTg.
Notably, the supervisory body requested clarification on the timing of the application of the five-tiered retail electricity pricing system for household consumption so that people can soon benefit from the new policy, meeting voters' expectations regarding the implementation of the issued electricity pricing structure.
You may also like
In addition, Vietnam Electricity Group ( EVN ) also proposed applying the new retail electricity pricing structure uniformly to all customer groups, instead of only applying it to tourist accommodation establishments and electric vehicle charging activities.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the amendment to the decision aims to expedite the implementation of the new pricing structure for different groups of electricity users, instead of allowing the existing regulations to remain in effect until the next adjustment of the average electricity price.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade emphasized that the application of the new retail electricity pricing structure is not an adjustment to the average electricity price. According to the proposal, the average retail electricity price will remain unchanged at 2,204.0655 VND/kWh.
To implement the new pricing structure, the Ministry of Industry and Trade will issue a decision stipulating the corresponding electricity selling prices, replacing the current regulations which were established based on the old tariff structure.
According to the draft, when the amended decision takes effect, Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg will be replaced by Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg along with the amendments and additions. The new electricity tariff structure will be applied from that time.
Why was the electricity tariff for household consumption reduced from six tiers to five?
According to the drafting documents for Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, the improvement of the residential electricity tariff stemmed from feedback from voters and National Assembly representatives regarding the tiered electricity pricing system.
Suggestions were made to review the current pricing structure to better reflect actual electricity usage, and to reduce the number of tiers to make it easier for people to monitor and manage their electricity costs. Some also proposed increasing the consumption limit for the first tier to 100 kWh and adjusting subsequent tiers to meet the growing demand for electricity.
Based on feedback received, the Ministry of Industry and Trade proposed reducing the residential electricity tariff from six tiers to five, while adjusting the price weight of each tier relative to the average retail electricity price. Compared to the previous six-tier structure, the new plan reduces the number of pricing tiers and expands the consumption range in some high-demand tiers.

articles.title: US has ‘two very different sets of intelligence reports’: Trump rules out Sunday strikes on Iran - The Times of India
articles.summary: US has ‘two very different sets of intelligence reports’: Trump rules out Sunday strikes on Iran  The Times of IndiaIran in ‘Advanced Stages’ of Planning Attacks Against Americans, Officials Say  The New York TimesU.S. Evacuates Mideast Outposts After Suspected Iranian Plot to Target Americans  WSJTrump Says US Has Two Different Sets of Intelligence on Iran  Bloomberg.comScoop: U.S. intel memo warns of "advanced" Iranian plots to kill officials abroad&nbsp...
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday ruled out an immediate military strike against Iran, saying Washington had no plans to launch an attack that day, even as conflicting intelligence assessments and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts continued to shape the US approach to Tehran.
"Would I tell you that? But the answer is no. There will not be a strike," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Michigan, responding to a question about whether military action against Iran could take place as soon as Sunday.
"We have two very different sets of intelligence reports," Trump said, describing the incoming information as "very advanced."
The president maintained that Washington was doing "well with Iran," although an unnamed US official told Israeli news channel i24NEWS that Trump was prepared to "shift gears on Iran" and that military strikes no longer appeared to be "a question of if, but of when."
The remarks came after Trump presented Tehran with a stark choice between reaching a diplomatic agreement and facing further military action.
"Do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off? That's the only question," Trump told Fox News, framing the next phase of the conflict as a choice between negotiations and escalating military operations.
Despite ruling out a strike on Sunday, Trump has continued to signal that Washington could pursue further military action if negotiations fail to produce an agreement.
Trump claims US controls Strait of Hormuz
Trump also asserted that American forces had established maritime dominance over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route and a major point of contention in the conflict with Iran.
"Remember, we now control the Hormuz Strait. They get nothing. Yes, we get everything." He maintained that commercial activity through the chokepoint had exceeded pre-war levels and described the US Navy's enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and shipping as "unbelievable."
On Saturday, Trump had suggested that Washington could either launch fresh military strikes or secure a comprehensive agreement with Tehran. He questioned whether Iran would honour any commitments under a potential deal, while arguing that either outcome would amount to an American victory.
Control over the Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of friction in the conflict, which erupted in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes. The confrontation has continued despite a ceasefire and a memorandum aimed at securing a final peace agreement.
Trump signals Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Turning to the war in Eastern Europe, Trump indicated that high-level diplomatic engagements involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine could take place soon.
"We're going to be having some pretty soon, and I think they both want to make a deal," he said, expressing optimism about the prospects of negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv.
Trump did not provide further details about the proposed engagements or specify when the talks would take place.
On Brazil's presidential election, the US president refrained from endorsing either candidate, saying his administration was "watching" the race.
Trump links European unrest to immigration
Trump also criticised immigration policies in European countries, linking protests and unrest in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain to what he described as inadequate border enforcement.
Contrasting the situation in Europe with US border controls, he claimed that the United States had prevented unauthorised crossings over the preceding 18 months.
"I closed the border. You know that we've had zero infiltration," Trump said, asserting that "zero illegal aliens" had entered the country during that period. He also claimed that previous US administrations had allowed millions of people to enter illegally.
Referring to his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron, Trump said he had previously warned the French leader about the consequences of immigration policies.
"'You are destroying France. You're letting people come in that hate your country.'" Trump said he had told Macron.
He also cited migrant arrivals in Spain as evidence of what he described as wider instability across Europe.
Trump accuses Taiwan of taking US chip industry
On semiconductor manufacturing and trade, Trump accused Taiwan of taking over the US chip industry through low-cost production, renewing his criticism of the island's position in the global semiconductor supply chain.
"They stole our chip business, all of it, 100%, because they made chips at a ridiculous price, and they just pushed them in," Trump said.
He argued that stronger executive leadership in Washington could have prevented broader tensions with China over trade and technology.
Trump's comments come amid continuing US efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing and address Washington's strategic competition with Beijing.

articles.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
articles.summary: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran  European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.
Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.
The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.
Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.
Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.
It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.
Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.
European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

"It places greater emphasis on processing and refining critical minerals. Particularly where Australia has, or can develop, a comparative advantage," she said. Australia is one of the world's largest suppliers of critical minerals, including rare earths used in defence and renewable energy. However, China dominates the complex and environmentally challenging refining stage of the supply chain.
Western nations are seeking to expand their critical minerals capabilities and diversify supplies as they move to reduce reliance on China for materials essential to the energy transition and national security. SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica, Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ten Costa Rican companies from the aerospace sector participated in an international trade event to identify new buyers and business partners, explore opportunities to join global supply chains, and follow up on existing business opportunities with key players in the international aerospace industry. Their participation was part of a broader strategy to expand the presence of Costa Rican suppliers in this sector. Another objective was to position Costa Rica as an attractive destination for new foreign direct investment (FDI) projects in the aerospace industry.
The companies participated in the NBAA Business Aviation Convention & Exhibition (NBAA-BACE), held from October 20 to 22 in Las Vegas, United States. Recognized as one of the leading international events for business aviation, the convention brought together more than 23,000 attendees and 1,000 exhibitors from 98 countries. This marked Costa Rica's sixth participation with an exhibition space at the event.
"The aerospace industry offers opportunities for Costa Rican companies to bring their capabilities in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and technology into highly specialized international supply chains. Our participation in NBAA also showcases an increasingly diverse range of capabilities, including software, automation, maintenance, and logistics. Our goal is to continue creating opportunities for more Costa Rican suppliers to enter this industry and move toward more sophisticated, higher value-added activities, while identifying investment opportunities that contribute to strengthening and developing the country's aerospace ecosystem," stated Laura López, CEO of the Trade and Investment Promotion Agency of Costa Rica (PROCOMER).
The delegation, led by PROCOMER and the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster (CRAC), included ten companies offering capabilities across different segments of the aerospace value chain: Avionyx and Novacomp, specializing in software and hardware; Soltek and Olympic Precision Machining, in precision machining; AASA, in automation; All Jets and Global Technik, in maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO); Aerologística and Interconexiones Multimodales de Carga (IMDC), in ground handling services; and GJ Cargo and IMDC, in logistics.
Companies Target Different Segments of the Aerospace Supply Chain
During NBAA-BACE, Costa Rican companies had access to businesses involved in manufacturing, maintenance, parts and accessories, design, engineering, software, and other specialized areas. Their participation provided an opportunity to follow up on potential business deals initiated during previous editions and establish new commercial contacts.
The event brought together operators, manufacturers, suppliers, and other industry stakeholders involved in purchasing decisions and the evaluation of solutions and technologies for the aerospace sector. The exhibition featured everything from commercial aircraft and private jets to eVTOL (electric vertical take-off and landing) aircraft, which are powered by electricity and capable of taking off and landing vertically.
"The Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster's participation in NBAA 2026 reflects the evolution and diversification of the capabilities our country offers to the global aerospace industry. In addition to its recognized expertise in advanced precision manufacturing and specialized engineering, Costa Rica continues to strengthen an increasingly comprehensive range of aviation-related services, including maintenance, repair, technical support, engineering solutions, corporate services, and capabilities that support aircraft operations," noted Esteban Carrillo, Executive Director of the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster (CRAC).
Carrillo added that "with PROCOMER's support, this participation helps foster strategic connections between Costa Rican companies and key industry players across international markets, creating new opportunities for business, investment, and collaboration."
Participation in NBAA was part of the international promotion and foreign direct investment attraction strategy developed by PROCOMER in collaboration with the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster. The strategy aims to strengthen the presence of Costa Rican suppliers in specialized markets and promote the country as a nearshoring destination for companies seeking manufacturing solutions and services to support their supply chains and aviation operations.
Throughout 2026, this strategy also brought companies from the sector to specialized international events, including the Aerospace Innovation Forum in Canada, Aerospace Meetings Querétaro in Mexico, and the Farnborough International Airshow in the United Kingdom.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election - The Guardian
articles.summary: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election  The GuardianNetanyahu Pushed for Attack on Iran Ahead of Israeli Election, Officials Say  The New York TimesNetanyahu says U.S. and Israel must topple Iranian regime  The Washington PostReport: Zamir the only security chief to oppose pre-election military action against Iran  The Times of IsraelNetanyahu Goes Into Full Panic Mode  The Atlantic
articles.full_text:
Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.title: Is India a “shadow transshipment” hub? The data says otherwise - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Is India a “shadow transshipment” hub? The data says otherwise  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy’s August 2026 report, ‘The Great Transshipment Scam,’ names India among the “Diversified Scale Leaders” of a 40-country network allegedly helping China evade the US tariffs. The claim rests on a striking chart: as China’s share of US imports fell after the 2018 Section 301 tariffs, the combined import share of India and 39 other countries rose in near mirror image. The report calls this “unlikely to be explained by chance alone.” For India, the evidence does not hold up.
A conflation at the core. The report flags any product where China’s US import share falls, a third country’s China imports rise, and that third country’s US exports rise—a correlation that cannot distinguish industrial upgrading from origin-laundering. It also conflates legitimate transshipment with illegal transshipment. Routing a genuinely transformed good through a third country is ordinary trade; falsely claiming that country as the origin to dodge duties is fraud. The report’s definition of “China-linked” goods—anything carrying “indicia” of Chinese content—risks capturing what global-value-chain integration is supposed to produce. Countries import Chinese components and add their own value before re-export. That is not evasion; it is manufacturing.
What India’s own numbers show. Between 2014 and 2024, India’s goods exports to the US grew 1.86 times, from $42.5 billion to $79.4 billion, but US exports to India grew even faster, 1.94 times. A rising two-way relationship, with India’s global exports also up 1.36-fold, is hard to square with a “mere pass-through” story tailored to one market.
More telling is what India now sells. Labour-intensive categories (such as textiles, apparel, gems and jewellery) that once dominated India’s US-bound exports have shrunk; textiles alone fell from 16.5% to 13% of the export basket. Capital- and skill-intensive sectors, such as machinery, electricals, pharmaceuticals, and chemicals, have captured that space, rising from 7.8% to 23.7%. This same shift appears in India’s exports to the world, not just the US, indicating that changes reflect structural transformation, not tariff arbitrage aimed at Washington.
The underlying capabilities back this up. UNCTAD’s productive-capacities index puts India’s score up from 40.3 to 46.4 over the decade, the highest gain among ASEAN peers. India’s export basket has also diversified across both products and markets, not narrowed into a few China-dependent corridors, while gross fixed capital formation in computers and electronics more than quadrupled between 2014 and 2022. None of these fits “screwdriver factories” built to disguise origin. Most decisively, OECD Trade in Value Added (TiVA) data show that between 2012 and 2022, as India’s gross exports to the US rose 1.87 times, the domestic value added embedded in those exports rose even faster, by 1.89 times. That is the opposite of what a transshipment hub, which adds minimal value while passing through someone else's content, would show.
A “scam,” or textbook arbitrage? Even setting India’s data aside, the framing deserves scrutiny of its first principles. When a government sets differentiated tariffs, firms respond predictably and rationally by rerouting trade and investment toward lower-tariff jurisdictions—a response that takes more than one form. Some firms may mislabel goods to disguise origin; that is fraud, worth punishing. Much of the “reallocation” the report documents, however, is ordinary business decision-making: factories relocating, suppliers diversifying, and genuine investment shifting to wherever tariffs are lowest. Calling all these a “scam” blurs a real enforcement problem with a lawful response economists would have forecast the moment the tariff schedule was drawn up. The report itself acknowledges the mechanism plainly—tariff differentials, it says, “are necessary to address differences in trading practices and levels of reciprocity, but they also create opportunities for arbitrage and evasion.” Having built the incentive into its own tariff design, the administration cannot then treat the predictable response as a foreign “scam.”
That is precisely what the WTO’s most-favoured-nation (MFN) principle was built to pre-empt. An MFN, rule-based tariff structure removes this arbitrage opportunity at its root by applying, with narrow negotiated exceptions, the same tariff to the same product regardless of source, so origin games yield no reward. Washington’s shift toward bilateral, “reciprocal” tariffs has reopened exactly the kind of gap MFN discipline was designed to close, and part of the cost now lands on the US Treasury too. A discriminatory tariff system creates room for discriminatory arbitrage; that is the system working as trade theory would predict, not a scandal manufactured by 40 “bad actor” countries. A durable fix lies at least as much in the rule-based, non-discriminatory framework Washington is weakening as in an “AI Detective Border” chasing the symptom.
India’s export data tell a story of competitiveness, not conspiracy. A tariff design that mistakes one for the other deserves at least as much scrutiny as the countries it accuses.
C. Veeramani is Director and RBI Chair Professor, Centre for Development Studies (CDS), Thiruvananthapuram; Himanshu Jaiswal is Consultant, Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP), New Delhi.

Thailand recorded a trade deficit of about US$5.86 billion in September 2026 as imports grew 50.4% year on year, outpacing a 24% rise in exports. Nantapong Chiralerspong, director-general of the Trade Policy and Strategy Office (TPSO), announced the September trade figures on October 26, 2026.
Thailand’s September exports amounted to US$38,438.9 million, or about 1.25 trillion baht, extending growth to a 27th consecutive month. Imports reached a record US$44,295.6 million, or about 1.46 trillion baht. The TPSO reported a deficit of US$5,856.6 million, equivalent to 209.402 billion baht.
Thailand’s trade deficit for January–September 2026 totalled US$43,693.9 million, or about 1.54 trillion baht, according to TPSO figures.
Thailand’s exports over the first nine months of 2026 rose 19.6% year on year to US$304,588.6 million, or about 9.76 trillion baht. Imports increased 37.8% to US$348,282.5 million, equivalent to about 11.3 trillion baht.
Nantapong attributed Thailand’s export strength to electronics demand linked to artificial intelligence (AI), data centres and global technology investment. Thailand’s role in global production chains helped support growth in electronics and electrical appliance shipments.
Thailand’s exports excluding oil-related products, gold and military goods grew 28.2% year on year in September 2026, according to the TPSO.
Nantapong also cited the International Monetary Fund’s assessment that Thailand was among the world’s major net exporters of AI-related hardware.
The United States remained Thailand’s largest export market, accounting for 26.5% of export value in September 2026, according to the TPSO’s market data.
Thailand’s agricultural and food export gains in September included natural rubber, frozen chicken and pet food, alongside fresh durians, mangosteens and longans.
Nantapong also pointed to a global manufacturing purchasing managers’ index of 53 in September 2026, a 55-month high, reflecting stronger new orders and export activity.
Nantapong said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continued to affect Thailand’s Middle Eastern export markets, while prolonged conflict weighed on demand. High energy and palm oil prices were also putting pressure on production costs, international transport and supply chains.
Nantapong said discussions with Thai commercial attachés overseas indicated that intermittent unrest in Europe had not yet directly affected Thailand’s overall exports.
European demonstrations could disrupt logistics networks and delay shipments if they escalated into strikes, Nantapong warned. Prolonged unrest could also weaken purchasing power and tourism in affected markets, putting pressure on Thai exports over the longer term.
Nantapong said the TPSO expected Thailand’s exports to grow by 15–16% in 2026, although an increase of 19% remained possible. Growth of 19% would take annual export value to approximately US$404,876.7 million, the highest on record.
Thailand’s Commerce Ministry will continue working with businesses, overseas commercial attachés and relevant agencies to support exports and respond to challenges in global markets.

articles.title: Implementing the RCEP Agreement: Leveraging Benefits and Enhancing Business Competitiveness - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Implementing the RCEP Agreement: Leveraging Benefits and Enhancing Business Competitiveness  Vietnam.vn

Export opportunities are wide open.
 The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) agreement, signed on November 15, 2020, between the 10 ASEAN countries and 5 partners – China, Japan, South Korea , Australia, and New Zealand – officially came into effect on January 1, 2022. The agreement creates a framework for large-scale regional economic cooperation, connecting economies at different levels of development while harmonizing certain trade rules, particularly rules of origin.
 One of the key advantages of RCEP is the cumulation of origin mechanism, which facilitates deeper participation of businesses in regional supply chains. Specifically, goods or materials that meet the RCEP origin requirements, when used as raw materials in another member country, can be considered to originate from the country where the final production or processing stage takes place, according to the relevant regulations. According to lawyer Le Hong Phuc, Senior Advisor at Rajah&Tann LCT Law Firm, the cumulation of origin mechanism allows businesses to use raw materials originating from member countries in their production processes, thereby expanding their ability to connect with supply sources and participate in regional production chains. 
 To take advantage of the benefits offered by the RCEP Agreement, businesses need to understand the relevant regulations and ensure they fully meet the requirements regarding origin.
 From an industry perspective, Ms. Le Hang, Deputy Secretary General of the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export (VASEP), stated that, in addition to the advantage of geographical proximity, RCEP creates further impetus for trade between Vietnam and China and ASEAN countries through preferential trade commitments and the ability to connect regional supply chains. Consumer demand in these markets has many similarities with the product structure and supply capacity of Vietnamese businesses. Therefore, when considering costs, profits, and business efficiency, many businesses choose China and ASEAN as key markets to diversify their outputs, reduce pressure from barriers, and better utilize the opportunities that RCEP offers.
 It is clear that the RCEP Agreement offers significant opportunities for Vietnamese exports. However, while it opens up more market access opportunities, the ability to utilize the agreement's benefits still depends on businesses' capacity in origin management, access to information, and compliance costs. In reality, the level of utilization of RCEP benefits is perceived as not commensurate with its potential. According to the report "Assessment of the Effectiveness of Vietnamese Businesses in Utilizing the RCEP Agreement," published by the Foreign Trade University in June 2026, a survey of 1,360 import-export businesses in 34 provinces and cities with import-export activities during 2023-2024 showed that one of the major obstacles is businesses' limited understanding of the agreement's regulations and lack of market information.
 Specifically, 39.3% of surveyed businesses stated they did not understand the RCEP regulations; 23.5% indicated a lack of market information was a major obstacle; while 19.6% worried about having to change their production and business processes to meet the requirements. These figures show that accessing a free trade agreement does not automatically mean the ability to effectively exploit the benefits. Businesses need to clearly understand the regulations, identify the applicable conditions for each product and market, and calculate the implementation costs to choose the most suitable option.
 Lawyer Le Hong Phuc stated that the biggest bottleneck preventing businesses from effectively exploiting RCEP commitments does not lie in the agreement lacking favorable commitments, but in the gap between the ability to access commitments on paper and the capacity to translate those commitments into actual economic benefits.
 Firstly, businesses have not effectively exploited tariff preferences due to a lack of understanding of rules of origin and eligibility conditions. Participation in RCEP does not automatically mean that all goods exported to member countries will benefit from preferential tariff rates. Businesses must correctly identify the HS code, compare it with the import market's tariff schedule, meet the specific rules of origin for each item, and follow the correct procedures for certifying origin. In some cases, the cost of proving origin and compliance may outweigh the tariff benefits, discouraging businesses from utilizing the preferences. This necessitates calculating both tariff benefits and related costs simultaneously, rather than solely relying on the tariff rate received.
 Furthermore, despite its broad membership, the tariff commitments and market access conditions within RCEP are not entirely uniform. The degree of benefit for a product can vary depending on the market, time, and applicable rules. Therefore, without sufficient information, businesses will struggle to identify markets where their products truly offer a competitive advantage. Another issue is compliance management capacity. Many businesses have not yet established sufficiently robust systems to control raw material sources, trace origins, meet technical standards, and fulfill contractual obligations with partners. 
 Investing in technology, research and development, product design, and branding will increase export opportunities for goods to RCEP markets.
 Enhancing compliance capacity and effectively utilizing commitments.
 Given the bottlenecks in exploiting the advantages of RCEP, experts suggest that to better utilize RCEP commitments, businesses need to implement a comprehensive set of solutions, with origin management being one of the crucial requirements, especially when using the cumulation of origin mechanism.
 According to lawyer Le Hong Phu, businesses need to create origin documentation for each product, including a list of raw materials, suppliers, HS codes, certificates of origin, and information about the production process. These documents need to be linked together so that businesses can provide explanations when customs authorities request inspections. Furthermore, businesses need to review their raw material purchase contracts and export contracts. The contracts should clearly stipulate the obligation to provide certificates of origin, ensure the accuracy of the information, the deadline for supplementing documents, and the responsibility for compensation if errors by one party cause the other party to lose tariff preferences or incur additional costs.
 At the same time, businesses need to establish internal verification procedures before requesting certificates of origin, clearly assigning responsibilities among the purchasing, production, import/export, and legal departments. Coordination between departments ensures that information on raw materials, production processes, and origin documentation is uniformly controlled. Emphasizing the need for early origin management, lawyer Le Hong Phuc stated: “ It is crucial to manage origin from the moment of selecting suppliers and designing production processes. If documentation is only checked when goods are ready for export, businesses may discover too late that the product does not meet the conditions for preferential treatment .”
 In particular, in the context of volatile global trade, for RCEP to truly become a driving force for enhancing competitiveness instead of just increasing export turnover, Vietnamese businesses need to shift from a mindset of exploiting tariff preferences in the short term to a strategy of deeper participation in regional value chains. In this context, legislation should not only be a tool for risk control but can also become a competitive advantage if integrated into investment, production, and business decisions.
 Accordingly, businesses are advised to simultaneously evaluate tariff commitments, rules of origin, and market access conditions to select the most suitable supply option. The choice should not be based solely on import tariffs but should also consider compliance costs, technical requirements, and the ability to meet rules of origin. Furthermore, it is necessary to strengthen legal capacity in supply chain management. Contracts with suppliers and distribution partners should specifically stipulate quality, origin, traceability, the right to inspect documents, information security, and liability in case of breaches. For long-term transactions, businesses need data on price adjustment mechanisms, changes in supply sources, and risk allocation when trade policies change.
 Furthermore, to retain more added value, businesses need to invest in technology, research and development, product design, branding, and intellectual property. If they only participate in low-margin processing, the benefits from expanding exports may not be commensurate with the increase in export value. Conversely, by mastering technology, product standards, and intellectual property rights, businesses have a better negotiating position with partners in the supply chain. Another requirement is to consider legal compliance as part of competitiveness. Businesses need to proactively monitor trade defense measures, standardize data, and build a risk management system.
 From the perspective of regulatory agencies, strengthening guidance for each industry, providing easily accessible market information, and supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in determining origin, accessing preferential treatment, and resolving trade disputes are also crucial. It recommended that banks develop specialised lending capabilities for semiconductors, hydrogen, data centres and battery storage, alongside products such as milestone-linked disbursements, receivables financing, equipment leasing and green loans.
The report identified renewable energy, semiconductors, green hydrogen and critical minerals as sectors suited to project finance and development finance institution-led funding, while electric vehicles and drones could benefit from asset financing and non-banking financial company lending.
