articles.title: Anthropic tries to outrun AI bubble with record-breaking IPO - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: Anthropic tries to outrun AI bubble with record-breaking IPO  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Anthropic is the next cab off the rank for mega-tech initial public offerings (IPO), and is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history.
An IPO involves a company asking big financial institutions and "mum and dad" investors for cash via the stock exchange.
Elon Musk's SpaceX played this game in June, raising $US85.7 billion ($121 billion), with a listing price of $US135.
It hit the boards of the Nasdaq and subsequently shot up to $US161, with unprecedented investor interest pushing the company to a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.
Prominent US analyst Dan Ives, in an interview from New York, said history was about to repeat itself with the listing of Anthropic.
"If you think about SpaceX obviously being the biggest IPO that we've seen this year, and this is, it's groundbreaking," the partner at Yorkville Ives said.
"It's a watershed event, not just for tech, but the AI revolution in terms of the role Anthropic plays."
Anthropic is a self-described AI safety and research company. Many Australians would be familiar with its Claude AI assistant product.
Locally, there's some healthy scepticism.
"Anthropic is trying to pull off a historic IPO right as the AI funding well is completely running dry," fund manager Roger Montgomer said.
On a wing and a prayer
When consumers spend on credit, it's often due to a lack of cash flow.
Companies are no different. They ask share investors (equity) and lenders (debt) for cash to operate.
The big difference is that firms will look to finance investments for future growth.
Investors, naturally, want to know they will not just get their money back but also have their investment grow over time.
This usually means the company needs to be generating a profit.
SpaceX was risky in that it was operating at a significant loss when it asked share investors for cash.
But it didn't matter. Elon Musk sold investors a dream, and the tech giant's Starlink operation acted as a much-needed cash cow for investors.
Anthropic is in a similar position, but its CEO Dario Amodei wants even more money.
The company is looking to raise about $US100 billion.
Analysts valued Anthropic earlier this year at $US2 trillion, but a recent financial results update showed the company revalued downwards to $US1.5 trillion.
There's no problem generating revenue — the company's third quarter revenue rose to $US16 billion.
"Anthropic's growth puts it in rarefied air," Betashares's head of investment strategy, Cameron Gleeson, said.
"Its annualised revenue run rate reportedly topped $US65 billion at the end of July, around seven times its level at the end of 2025, and many expect it to approach $US100 billion by year-end.
"It has overtaken OpenAI in business adoption, where much of the potential to monetise AI lies, and achieved this with a workforce of around 5,300."
Spending bonanza
Anthropic's costs are damaging its bottom line.
Like many big tech companies, Anthropic is building its business rapidly to meet expected demand.
It means building cloud computing infrastructure, AI training chips, and data centre capacity.
In the second quarter alone, it spent $US5.6 billion on computing power to run its Claude models.
Adding salt to a wound, the cost of debt, which big tech companies are increasingly chasing, is becoming more expensive as inflation affects the global economy and interest rates rise.
The fundamental problem is that if, for example, the demand for SpaceX and Anthropic's products does not justify the spending being undertaken by these companies, the entire artificial intelligence trade is at risk of collapsing.
"[It's] basically playing chicken with a market where Elon Musk is warning that debt is impossible to get, over 200 over-leveraged neoclouds are going belly up, and [the failed] Firmus IPO," Roger Montgomery said.
In other words, the fund manager believes investors who want the huge artificial intelligence trade to keep going will invest in Anthropic or risk a Wall Street crash.
"I think they're trying to get ahead of the bubble possibly bursting,"
he said.
And while Ives is confident the IPO will be a success, he says the company has not yet produced the sort of numbers that would justify its current valuation.
"For investors, they're going to basically need to look past this year," he said.
"I think Anthropic, being that they're the centrepiece of the AI revolution, you're going to see probably a strong appetite for this offering."
Loading
Australia at the table
As with the SpaceX IPO, Australians will be able to apply for shares in Anthropic.
Macquarie Capital will act as sub-underwriter and Australian coordinator for the listing.
Ives says it's up to investors to weigh up the risks.
"We're all going into it. Whether it's here in the US, Australia, wherever we are … we're all going into this fourth industrial revolution together,"
he said.
"And there's a lot of opportunity and growth, but there's also risk."
You could argue this is modern capitalism's biggest ever test.
Massive AI tech companies have a spending addiction. They need the cash to invest to hyper-scale, to try and produce the amount of product or service necessary to meet forecast demand.
Now, having largely exhausted debt markets, they're looking to raise equity.
Simply put, if something disrupts this trade, there is no government on the planet, nor central bank, that could clean up the damage caused without major disruption to the global economy.

articles.title: Thai farm exports weaken as electronics power record September shipments - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thai farm exports weaken as electronics power record September shipments  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s agricultural and agro-industrial exports fell 1.9% in the first nine months of 2026 as high production costs and intense global competition weighed on key products, even as booming electronics shipments pushed the country’s overall exports to record levels.
Exports in September reached a record US$38.44 billion, up 24% year on year and marking a 27th consecutive month of growth.
Imports, however, surged 50.4% to an all-time high of US$44.30 billion, leaving Thailand with a trade deficit of US$5.86 billion for the month.
For January to September, exports totalled US$304.59 billion, up 19.6%, while imports rose 37.8% to US$348.28 billion. The nine-month trade deficit consequently widened to US$43.69 billion.
Nuntapong Jiralertpong, director-general of the Trade Policy and Strategy Office (TPSO), said the acceleration in September exports was driven largely by electronics as Thailand benefited from its position in global technology supply chains.
The International Monetary Fund has identified Thailand as one of the world’s four largest net exporters of artificial-intelligence-related hardware, alongside South Korea, Malaysia and Taiwan.
Nuntapong said the sharp rise in imports should not be viewed solely as evidence of stronger domestic consumption.
Raw materials and semi-finished goods accounted for 41.7% of imports, while capital goods represented another 33.5%.
Major imports included computers and equipment, electrical machinery, integrated circuits, machinery and components, much of which feeds into domestic manufacturing and subsequent exports.
Fuel accounted for 11.9% of imports, consumer goods 8.7%, vehicles 3.2%, and arms, military supplies and other items about 1%.
He said the import structure showed that a substantial portion of the increase was linked to investment and production rather than household demand alone.
Agricultural and agro-industrial exports rose 2.5% in September, extending growth for a second month.
Pure agricultural exports increased 8.1%, while agro-industrial goods fell 2.7%.
Products recording declines included wheat products and other prepared foods, sugar, animal and vegetable fats and oils, fresh, chilled and frozen fish, and coffee.
The longer-term picture remained weaker.
Agricultural and agro-industrial exports during the first nine months were valued at US$39.92 billion, down 1.9% year on year.
Among major products, canned tuna exports slipped 0.4% to US$3.91 billion, natural rubber fell 2.5% to US$3.71 billion and rice dropped 16.6% to US$2.96 billion.
Cassava-product exports declined 28.4% to US$1.70 billion, while sugar fell 21.8% to US$1.89 billion.
Industrial exports increased 25.4% in September, extending their run of growth to 30 consecutive months.
Strong performers included computers and components, telephones and related equipment, and integrated circuits.
Industrial exports over the first nine months reached US$255.18 billion, up 23%.
Motor-vehicle exports were worth US$16.90 billion, down 0.9%, while vehicle parts and accessories rose 3.3% to US$12.97 billion.
Hard-disk-drive exports increased 18.9% to US$10.43 billion and integrated circuits gained 19% to US$10.06 billion. Air-conditioner exports rose 1.6% to US$5.94 billion.
Exports to Thailand’s main markets remained strong in September.
Shipments to the United States surged 50.1%, while exports to China increased 18.4%, Japan 19%, the European Union 35%, the five major ASEAN markets 27% and Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam collectively 16.6%.
Among secondary markets, exports to Australia rose 37.7%, Latin America 29.3%, Africa 5.2% and the United Kingdom 14.6%.
Exports to Russia and the Commonwealth of Independent States fell 12.4%, South Asia declined 2.7% and the Middle East dropped 8.7%.
Full-year exports could grow 15–16%
TPSO expects export growth to remain positive during the final three months of the year and sees full-year expansion of 15–16% as achievable, above its previous central estimate.
To achieve 15% growth, Thailand would need exports worth US$86.68 billion during the fourth quarter, or an average of about US$28.89 billion a month.
Growth of 16% would require fourth-quarter exports of about US$90.08 billion, or US$30.03 billion a month.
If the electronics cycle remains exceptionally strong and investment in AI infrastructure continues to accelerate, TPSO sees a possibility of export growth reaching 19%, which would take annual shipments to about US$404.88 billion and set another record.
For 2027, however, export growth is provisionally forecast at only 2–4% because of the much higher comparison base, although global economic expansion and continuing investment in AI are expected to provide support.
Nuntapong said Thailand was also monitoring protests and labour action in Europe, including France and Italy.
Although there had been no clear short-term effect on Thai exports, prolonged strikes or disruptions to production and transport could affect supply chains and eventually weaken demand for Thai goods.
The risks would increase if labour disputes persisted long enough to slow production, employment or consumer demand in major European markets.
Assoc Prof Aat Pisanwanich of Rangsit University’s Faculty of Economics said Thailand’s exports to the United States were likely to remain strong in the final quarter while uncertainty persisted over the pending Thailand-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.
Thailand and the United States remain in the final stages of those negotiations.
Aat said exporters had an incentive to accelerate shipments before future tariff conditions became clearer.
Technology and innovation-related industrial products, including communications equipment, smartphones, electronics and electrical appliances, were likely to remain important drivers of export growth.
Agricultural exports, however, faced a more difficult environment.
Aat said Thai farm products carry relatively high production costs and prices and face strong competition from other producers, particularly Vietnam, which exports many of the same commodities.
Rice exports, he noted, had already been weakening for seven to eight months.
Finding entirely new markets would also be difficult because global agricultural competition remained intense.
Aat said Thailand should move more agricultural production away from raw commodities and towards processed products with greater added value and clearer differentiation.
Premium markets including the United States, Europe and Japan place greater emphasis on quality and standards, while China, India, Africa and the Middle East represent important mid-tier markets.
He said parts of the Middle East could also develop into premium markets for Thai processed agricultural products.
Although Thailand already produces high-quality processed food and agricultural brands, he said overseas marketing and recognition remained weaknesses.
Greater attention was therefore needed on distribution channels, branding and international marketing strategies.
Aat expects exports to continue expanding during the final quarter, supported by two main factors: exporters bringing forward shipments because of uncertainty over US tariff policy, and higher overseas demand during the Christmas and New Year period.
However, stronger exports are also likely to be accompanied by rising imports as manufacturers bring in additional raw materials, machinery and goods to meet production and seasonal demand.
He regarded full-year export growth of about 15–17% as achievable, while describing 19% as a more demanding target dependent on US tariff developments, global demand and continued momentum in technology-related industrial exports.

Banking as a Service on Both Sides of the Atlantic
What Cross-Border Fintechs Need To Know
- October 27, 2026
The landscape of Banking-as-a-Service (“BaaS”) represents one of the most consequential structural questions facing fintechs with global ambitions. As cross-border fintech activity accelerates and regulatory scrutiny of bank-fintech partnerships intensifies across major markets, understanding how BaaS obligations are allocated in key markets such as the United States, United Kingdom and European Union has become essential for any firm seeking to build durable, compliant partnerships at scale.
This article examines the structural features of BaaS in each of these jurisdictions, identifies where they converge and diverge and offers a framework for building a scalable, cross-border compliance program.
United States: Sponsor-Bank Access and Oversight
In the U.S. market, the defining architectural feature of BaaS is the centrality of the chartered sponsor bank. Fintechs access payments infrastructure, deposit accounts, card products and lending not through their own licenses, but through partnerships with licensed banks that retain the charter and the regulatory accountability that comes with it. This is a critical distinction: the commercial arrangement between a bank and a fintech does not transfer the bank’s regulatory obligations. The bank remains responsible for identifying, assessing, monitoring and controlling risks arising from the relationship in accordance with safety-and-soundness, consumer protection and compliance requirements.1
What this means is that fintechs operating in the U.S. should expect to be subject to a robust oversight regime designed to give the sponsor bank the visibility it needs to fulfill its own obligations. This includes providing relevant customer and transaction data, risk and compliance reporting and evidence that controls are operating effectively. Banks may also retain audit and testing rights, require approval over material program changes and reserve the authority to restrict or terminate the partnership when risks are not adequately managed. The regulatory actions taken against sponsor banks in recent years, reflecting supervisory findings and enforcement activity across multiple institutions, illustrate precisely what happens when oversight capabilities fail to keep pace with the scale or complexity of fintech partnerships.
A successful U.S. BaaS partnership demands more than a commercially compelling product. It requires the fintech to maintain the controls, documentation, data capabilities and operational transparency necessary to support effective bank oversight and to demonstrate that those capabilities are functioning as intended.
United Kingdom: Direct Authorization, Customer Outcomes and Resilience
The UK presents a structurally different picture. A fintech may operate in the UK under its own regulatory authorization (as an e-money institution, a payment institution or under another permission set granted by the Financial Conduct Authority (“FCA”)) while partnering with banks to access safeguarded funds, settlement infrastructure, payment-system access or other regulated services. The fintech is not simply a downstream distributor of a bank’s charter; it may itself be a regulated entity with direct obligations. This creates a more layered accountability structure, where both parties carry regulatory responsibilities that must be carefully coordinated.
Two themes dominate the UK regulatory environment in ways that directly shape BaaS partnerships. The first is customer outcomes. The FCA’s Consumer Duty requires in-scope regulated firms to deliver good outcomes for retail consumers,2 and where a fintech supports the delivery of a product or service, the regulated firm must still meet its applicable obligations. Accountability for those outcomes is not transferred simply because aspects of the product or service are delivered through third parties. Fintechs may therefore need to demonstrate to their banking partners that their technology, processes and customer interactions actively support good customer outcomes, not merely that they avoid causing harm.
The second theme is operational resilience. Cyber incidents, outages and transaction-processing disruptions involving a fintech can affect its banking partner and, depending on the circumstances, trigger regulatory reporting obligations.3 Fintechs must be prepared to support effective incident identification, escalation, reporting and remediation. The effectiveness of that oversight is becoming an increasingly important area of supervisory focus.
European Union: Direct Obligations and an Expanding Regulatory Perimeter
The EU framework introduces yet another dimension of complexity: an expanding regulatory perimeter that can impose obligations directly on fintechs, not merely on their regulated financial institution partners. The Digital Operational Resilience Act (“DORA”) strengthens Information and Communications Technology (“ICT”) and third-party risk management requirements for financial entities and even permits direct oversight of certain critical ICT service providers – a significant development for fintechs that function as technology infrastructure within BaaS arrangements.4 Beyond DORA, three additional frameworks can create further obligations depending on the specific activities involved: the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (“MiCA”), which applies to firms issuing or providing services related to crypto-assets;5 the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, which introduces risk-based requirements for AI systems used in regulated contexts;6 and the evolving AML framework, which continues to expand its scope and harmonize requirements across member states.7 Not all of these frameworks will apply to every BaaS arrangement. Their relevance depends on the products, services and technologies involved, but fintechs operating in the EU must assess their applicability carefully.
This broader regulatory perimeter has a cascading effect on BaaS relationships. As fintechs become subject to more direct regulatory obligations, their financial institution partners simultaneously need greater visibility into fintech operations, including the controls, data and documentation necessary to effectively oversee the relationship. The EU environment therefore demands that fintechs understand not only what obligations apply directly to their own activities, but also how those activities shape the regulatory responsibilities and oversight needs of their partners. This dual awareness is what distinguishes a fintech that is merely compliant from one that is genuinely partnership-ready.
Comparing Markets: Structural Differences, Consistent Expectations
Viewing all three markets together reveals a pattern that is both clarifying and strategically important. The structural differences are real and consequential. In the U.S., the sponsor bank is the central gateway to regulated banking infrastructure and the fintech’s primary compliance obligation is to support the bank’s oversight capabilities. In the UK, fintechs may hold their own authorization while using banks for specific regulated functions, with particular emphasis on demonstrating good customer outcomes and operational resilience. In the EU, regulatory obligations are shaped by each party’s specific activities and role within the arrangement, with an expanding perimeter that increasingly reaches fintechs directly.
There is still convergence despite these structural differences. Across all three markets, regulators expect that financial products delivered through BaaS arrangements are underpinned by effective governance, controls, information flows and oversight capabilities and that the parties to those arrangements can demonstrate as much. This convergence is not coincidental. It reflects a shared regulatory philosophy: that the structural form of a partnership does not determine where accountability ends.
Recommendations for Cross-Border Fintechs With BaaS Partnerships
For fintechs operating across these three markets, the strategic challenge is building a compliance framework that is both rigorous and scalable. Simply replicating one market’s framework in another is insufficient, but building entirely separate frameworks for every jurisdiction creates unnecessary complexity and fragmentation. The more effective approach involves three interconnected priorities.
- Establish a Common Control Baseline. Across all three markets, regulators expect effective governance, risk management and compliance controls. A well-designed baseline, covering areas such as customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, data governance, incident management and third-party oversight can serve as the foundation for compliance in each jurisdiction, reducing duplication and creating consistency at the core of the program.
- Supplement That Baseline With Targeted Jurisdictional Enhancements. In the U.S., this means building the data-sharing, reporting and audit-support capabilities that sponsor banks require. In the UK, it means designing processes and customer interactions that can demonstrate compliance with Consumer Duty and support operational resilience obligations. In the EU, it means assessing applicability under DORA, MiCA, the AI Act and the evolving AML framework and building the documentation and evidence infrastructure those regimes require.
- Design the Entire Control Environment for Demonstrability. Having appropriate policies and controls is necessary but not sufficient. Firms must be able to provide the data, documentation, testing results, reporting and evidence of remediation needed to demonstrate that those controls actually operate effectively. This capability serves a dual purpose: it supports the fintech’s own compliance obligations while enabling banks and other regulated partners to exercise the meaningful oversight that regulators in all three markets expect.

articles.title: Mapping Green Transition Of Asia Pacific Economies - Mirage News
articles.summary: Mapping Green Transition Of Asia Pacific Economies  Mirage News
articles.full_text:
Countries in the Asia Pacific can accelerate the shift to clean energy while building competitive local industries as long as policies don't slow access to affordable technologies, a new report has found.
Researchers from The University of Queensland and University of California (UC) San Diego have examined clean technology deployment, trade and manufacturing investment across 9 Asia Pacific economies, including Australia.
UQ's Professor Christoph Nedopil said clean technology manufacturing investment announcements across the 9 countries reached more than $15.5 billion ($11 billion USD) in the first half of 2026, led by Indonesia and India.
"Across the Asia Pacific, countries are not following a single roadmap," Professor Nedopil said.
"We found there are distinct transition pathways, depending on the country's domestic industry, trade and energy priorities.
"For example, Australia's renewable energy expansion relies heavily on imported technologies similar to Pakistan and the Philippines, while Malaysia and Thailand are export-oriented.
"Meanwhile India is building manufacturing capacity, primarily for domestic use.
"The risk for import-dependant countries like Australia is an overreliance on external suppliers, but the opportunity lies in developing positions in supply chains and value-added activities."
Professor Nedopil said India, Australia and Vietnam lead the region in adopting renewable energy generation.
"India added 172 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity between 2015 and 2025, and Australia managed to add 48 GW of capacity, despite limited domestic clean technology manufacturing," he said.
Associate Professor Michael Davidson from UC San Diego said China remained the dominant supplier of imported clean technologies for most economies.
"Ninety-nine per cent of Pakistan's solar equipment imports came from China in 2025," Dr Davidson said.
"China also supplied the remaining Asia Pacific economies in the study with more than 60 per cent of their battery imports and New Energy Vehicles, except for batteries to Malaysia.
"Conversely, the United States is a dominant buyer of clean technology from the Asia Pacific, with Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand sending more than half of their solar exports to the US.
"Changing United States trade policies also create uncertainty for export-oriented manufacturers."
Professor Nedopil said investment announcements and trade surpluses did not necessarily translate into operating factories, local jobs or technological capability.
"Access to affordable imports can speed up the energy transition but building competitive local manufacturing requires sustained demand, strong supply chains and ongoing innovation," he said.
"The challenge is creating lasting economic value without slowing the shift to clean energy."
Collaboration and acknowledgements
Professor Nedopil is the lead for Asia Pacific Industry Transitions in the UQ Business School .
Dr Davidson is an Associate Professor in the School of Global Policy and Strategy, and the Jacobs School of Engineering at University of California San Diego.
The research was supported by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund.

articles.title: Can You Invest in Temu in 2026? - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: Can You Invest in Temu in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
Temu has become one of the most downloaded shopping apps in the U.S. since launching in late 2022, thanks to ultra-low prices, viral marketing, and rapid expansion into new product categories. Its fast rise, and growing rivalry with Shein, has sparked a lot of curiosity, not just from shoppers, but from investors too.
Below, we’ll break down Temu’s outlook, how to invest indirectly today, and what to consider before putting money behind the fast-growing platform.
Is Temu publicly traded?
Temu is not a publicly traded company. Instead, it operates under PDD Holdings (PDD -1.15%), a global e-commerce company based in China.
When will Temu IPO?
Temu didn't have an IPO on the calendar as of 2026. As it's still in the early stages of its growth, the company likely won't seek to complete an IPO any time soon. PDD Holdings launched the company in late 2022 to help drive its growth. Before considering an IPO, it will likely want to continue supporting its new initiative and help it grow into a more mature company, including reaching solid profitability.
PDD Holdings might never complete an IPO of Temu. It could hold on to the company indefinitely as a growth driver for its investors. Another option it could consider is to spin off a portion or all of Temu to its shareholders instead of completing an IPO.
Alternatives to Temu stock
You can't buy Temu stock yet because it hasn't completed its IPO. However, you can gain exposure to the fast-fashion and apparel trends driving its growth while you wait for an IPO.
Here's a look at some alternatives to consider while you wait to see whether the company will ever go public.
PDD Holdings
PDD Holdings launched Temu in September 2022, making it the most direct way to invest in Temu. PDD Holdings' investors can benefit from the growth of Temu and its other businesses, which include the popular e-commerce platform Pinduoduo.
Amazon
Temu is putting a lot of pressure on Amazon (AMZN +0.44%) by selling similar products at lower prices. However, Amazon is a behemoth in the e-commerce space. It has the financial firepower to compete even more directly with rivals like Temu and Shein by lowering prices and increasing its marketing spend.
Amazon could afford to do that because it has a major higher-margin growth driver in its cloud computing business. The business, which is capitalizing on the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, could help power Amazon's stock price even as it battles Temu.
Alibaba
Alibaba (BABA +0.61%) competes with Amazon and PDD Holdings in the global e-commerce market, selling a range of goods at similar prices. PDD's Temu (and its Pinduoduo platform) are also putting pressure on Alibaba. However, it has already battled competitors across its much longer operating history.
It also has several other business units to drive growth, including fintech Ant Group and a cloud computing unit. It offers diverse revenue streams and growth opportunities that put it in a strong position to compete with upstarts like Temu and Shein.
How to buy stocks similar to Temu
Investors who want to buy one of these Temu alternatives can purchase shares in most brokerage accounts. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to invest in stocks like Temu.
- Open your brokerage account: Log in to your brokerage account where you handle your investments. If you don't have one yet, take a look at our favorite brokers and trading platforms to find the right one for you.
- Search for the stock: Enter the ticker of the stock you'd like to buy into the search bar to bring up the stock's trading page.
- Decide how many shares to buy: Consider your investment goals and how much of your portfolio you want to allocate to this stock.
- Select order type: Choose between a market order to buy at the current price or a limit order to specify the maximum price you're willing to pay.
- Submit your order: Confirm the details and submit your buy order.
- Review your purchase: Check your portfolio to ensure your order was filled as expected and adjust your investment strategy accordingly.
Is Temu profitable?
While PDD Holdings is a publicly traded company, it doesn't currently break out Temu's financial results. That said, PDD reported slightly weaker-than-expected sales in the second quarter of 2026, with overall revenue up roughly 16.6%.
The business unit isn't likely to be profitable yet. According to an article by The Information, Temu is losing significant money as it spends heavily to win customers in the U.S.
The company planned to spend heavily on U.S. advertising while subsidizing the high cost of international shipping, but the Trump administration tariffs have caused it to pull back on its spending. PDD Holdings reported an almost 50% drop in profits in May 2025 as a response to President Trump's tariffs, making Temu's products potentially unprofitable to sell. Even so, PDD Holdings is still solidly profitable. The company reported its Q2 results in mid-2025, posting $3.8 billion in net income.
The short answer to whether Temu is profitable is probably not yet, but its parent company is still sitting well into the black.
Should you invest in Temu?
While you can't invest directly in Temu since it hasn't completed an IPO, you can buy shares of its parent company, PDD Holdings. That company gives you exposure to the growth of Temu and its leading Chinese e-commerce platform, Pinduoduo. PDD Holdings is using the profits of Pinduoduo and its other businesses to grow Temu.
PDD Holdings could have significant upside potential. Temu's rapid expansion is driving significant revenue growth. While Temu's losses will weigh on its profitability, PDD remains highly profitable, delivering strong earnings growth across its other operations. So, it could be a compelling long-term investment.
However, PDD Holdings isn't without risk. It operates in China, which carries geopolitical risks. Meanwhile, it's spending heavily to subsidize Temu's growth to compete against large rivals like Amazon, Alibaba, and JD.com (JD -0.47%). Competitors could ramp up their spending to wrestle customers back from Temu, potentially stunting its growth and hurting PDD Holdings' profitability.
Can you invest in Temu through ETFs?
Many people prefer to passively invest in a company or trend rather than actively pick a portfolio of stocks to manage. Investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) makes that easy.
Although you can't use ETFs to invest passively in Temu, you can use them to gain exposure to its parent, PDD Holdings. According to ETF.com, 143 U.S.-traded ETFs held 70.9 million shares of PDD Holdings in late 2026. The following ETFs had the largest allocation to PDD Holdings:
- Global X MSCI China Consumer Discretionary ETF (CHIQ +0.19%): The fund tracks large- and mid-cap consumer discretionary companies in China. The ETF held 8.85% of its assets in PDD Holdings stock, its largest weighting. The fund had an ETF expense ratio of 0.65%.
- Invesco China Technology ETF (CQQQ -0.57%): The ETF tracks investable Chinese technology stocks. The fund's allocation in PDD Holdings equaled 11.58%. The ETF had a 0.65% expense ratio.
- ProShares Online Retail ETF (ONLN -0.41%): The fund focuses on online retailers. PDD Holdings made up 4.44% of its total holdings. The ETF has a 0.58% expense ratio.
The bottom line
While you can't buy Temu shares directly, you can invest in its parent company, PDD Holdings, which also owns the leading Chinese e-commerce platform Pinduoduo. The profitability of the platform and its other businesses gives PDD the funds to invest heavily in expanding Temu as it competes against large rivals like Amazon. Although PDD carries its share of risk, it could be a great investment, especially as Temu grows and eventually starts generating revenue.

articles.summary: Texas Roadhouse Responds to Customer’s Viral Claims That He Was Given $20 Steak Instead of the $30 Cut He Ordered 3 Times  YahooMan says Texas Roadhouse served him $20 steak instead of pricier filet multiple times  Fox NewsTexas Roadhouse responds to customer's viral claim he was given cheaper steak 3 times  WBFFKenneth Card, loyal Texas Roadhouse customer from Illinois, was served $20 steak despite ordering the $30 one  Hindustan TimesViral: He ordered a ...
articles.full_text:
NEED TO KNOW
- Kenneth Card claimed that he was served a sirloin instead of the filet mignon he ordered on three separate occasions at a Texas Roadhouse in Forsyth, Ill.
- Texas Roadhouse said Card's complaint was "made right" by its team and that it could not confirm multiple incidents.
- Card, who says he used to work in restaurants, sparked an online debate after sharing a video detailing his experience.
A Texas Roadhouse customer is claiming that the restaurant served him a cheaper steak than he ordered.
On Oct. 5, Kenneth Card shared a TikTok video, which now has over 31,000 views, calling out the steakhouse chain and claiming he was served a less expensive steak than he ordered three times.
In his video, Card said he ordered an 8-oz. filet mignon at the Forsyth, Ill. location of the steakhouse chain before being served a sirloin steak instead.
"I said, 'Excuse me, I think I got the wrong steak,'" Card recalled in the video, adding that the server went to get a "second opinion" before returning and confirming it was a sirloin steak.
Card said he told the waiter he went to the restaurant weekly for a year, and this was the third time the issue occurred.
He told Fox News Digital the staff corrected the mistake the first time it happened, and that he didn't complain the second time it occurred.
Card said in his video that he told a manager it was the third time he received a sirloin instead of the filet he ordered.
He claimed that the manager looked at him as if he was "stupid or crazy" and said it was "impossible" because the steak goes through a manager in the back.
Card said when he brought up the current mistake, the manager was unable to respond.
"While we can't confirm this happened on multiple occasions, when Mr. Card brought this to our attention; it was made right by our team," a spokesperson for Texas Roadhouse said in a statement shared with PEOPLE.
"We have processes in place to double-check food for quality and accuracy before it leaves the kitchen," they added. "If a guest receives the wrong item or is charged incorrectly, we encourage them to let a member of our team know so we can make it right."
In his video, Card said that he was a cook "for many years" and had experience with handling steaks.
"I know [the] difference between a ribeye, a filet, a t-bone, New York strip, all that crap," he said in the video. "Whenever I go out to eat, I know what I get."
Card previously worked in hotel and restaurant kitchens, per Fox News Digital.
"Y'all be careful what y'all ordering and what you pay for because sometimes you order a filet, you'd be getting a sirloin," he told his viewers. "It's like a $10 steak versus $35."
Per the Texas Roadhouse location's website, an 8-oz. sirloin costs $19.49, and the 8-oz. Dallas filet costs $29.99.
"Talking about getting ripped off!" Card wrote in the caption of his TikTok, also writing in text overlaying the video, "Texas Roadhouse shame on you!"
Card did not immediately reply to PEOPLE's request for comment.
Some users sympathized with Card's position in the comments section of his video.
"This has been going on for years," one person claimed.
Another added, "They've done this to me many times. Ordered New York strip or ribeye and I get a sirloin."
However, others questioned Card's point of view.
"I've never had an issue with Texas roadhouse," one commenter wrote.
"Why do you keep going back if this continues to happen?" another asked.
"I think I'm done going in there," Card told Fox News Digital.
He told the outlet he wanted to ensure that customers got what they paid for.

Three noteworthy names appear in the list of investors: Groupe Renault made its first investment, Chery Automobile increased its stake, and domestic storage leader ChangXin Memory Technologies participated in this round.
Also worth noting is the customer list of XHEART's X7 chip. The first vehicle model equipped with this chip is SAIC Volkswagen ID.ERA 9X, and subsequent coverage is planned for SAIC MG, Roewe, General Motors Cadillac, and some new energy and fuel vehicle models under Chery.
How could a chip company established only three years ago and with mass production deployment on vehicles for less than a year secure investments from storage giants and orders from domestic and overseas automakers at the same time? The key behind this lies in its "blood tie" with autonomous driving company Momenta.
Cao Xudong, Founder and CEO of Momenta, publicly stated at the 2026 Physical AI and World Model Conference opening on October 20: "XHEART, the 'sister company' of Momenta, defines chips around the needs of large models, which is expected to increase performance by about 10 times under the same cost and power consumption. Its next-generation X9 chip will further expand the scale of edge-side models by 100 times."
He summarized the rhythm of improving intelligent driving safety as "Intelligent Driving Moore's Law", and pointed out that the expansion of model scale requires chip support. The cooperation logic with XHEART is to drive chip design with model requirements and support model expansion with chips.
Demands of the Three Investors
XHEART was founded in December 2023, headquartered in Suzhou. Li Jun, its legal representative and chairman, is the former head of the chip department of Momenta. Cao Xudong and Xia Yan, core members of Momenta's founding team, hold shares in XHEART indirectly through the controlling shareholder. From the perspective of equity structure, the two companies do not have a direct subordinate relationship, but from the perspective of business and founding team background, XHEART was spun off from Momenta's chip project for independent financing.
This "blood tie" is directly reflected at the product level. During the planning and design phase of the X7 chip, the team conducted in-depth collaboration with the Momenta team, embedding algorithm understanding into the chip architecture. In August 2026, XHEART, together with Momenta and automotive operating system supplier QNX, jointly announced the development of a mass-production-oriented autonomous driving platform that meets global safety standards: Momenta provides full-stack algorithms, XHEART provides the automotive-grade SoC X7, and QNX provides a safety operating system.
From the project designation to mass production deployment on vehicles, XHEART took less than three years, which is faster than the usual 3 to 4-year R&D cycle in the automotive-grade chip industry.
The "blood tie" background with Momenta also explains why Groupe Renault, Chery Automobile and ChangXin Memory Technologies all appear in XHEART's investor list. The three investors have different demands, but they all value the same thing: a chip company that can hardwareize algorithm capabilities holds a unique position amid the trend of intelligent driving solutions moving toward "hardware-software integration".
Relevant personnel from XHEART stated that ChangXin Memory Technologies is a giant in the domestic storage industry. This investment marks its investment case for chip companies with automotive industry background, which is expected to help XHEART gain quotation and supply advantages against the backdrop of rising memory prices.
The equity participation of Groupe Renault and Chery Automobile is regarded by XHEART as "a key step for going global". Groupe Renault is a leading European automaker, and Chery Automobile is a pioneer of Chinese independent brands expanding overseas. The equity binding with the two parties means that XHEART's chips need to not only meet the demands of the Chinese market, but also comply with European regulations and safety standards.
"The participation of QNX is to help meet global safety thresholds. For Renault, investing in a Chinese chip company with mass production customer endorsements adds an alternative supply chain option in addition to Nvidia and Horizon Robotics," a relevant person in charge of a Beijing-based intelligent driving company told Economic Observer. For Chery, deep binding with chip suppliers is aimed at gaining more say in the definition of intelligent driving solutions.
Why Momenta Has to "Develop Chips"
Momenta is a leading domestic autonomous driving algorithm company, with a cumulative mass production delivery volume of more than 1.3 million units and a cumulative driving mileage of nearly 200 billion kilometers. However, the ceiling of algorithm development is approaching. Cao Xudong once said that software algorithms need to reach a sales volume of 4 million units to achieve economies of scale.
Self-controllable chips are the path to break this ceiling, and also the only way to get rid of dependence on external chip suppliers. Momenta's algorithms currently run on multiple chip platforms such as Nvidia, Horizon Robotics and Qualcomm, but the procurement cost, adaptation cycle and underlying optimization permission of each chip are not in its own hands.
"Chips are one of the most profitable links in the intelligent driving solutions. The gross profit margin of intelligent driving chips is generally between 40% and 50%, and the gross profit margin of Nvidia's intelligent driving chips even exceeds 60%. The gross profit of software solutions is inherently low, and automakers keep pushing down prices. All participants want to take the profit of the chip sector for themselves," the above-mentioned relevant person in charge of the Beijing-based intelligent driving company said, "At the same time, selling chips and solutions as a package brings higher profits and reduces the risk of being replaced by automaker customers."
The continuous iteration of intelligent driving algorithms requires a custom-built chip to support it. "Now everyone is saying that simply stacking computing power is useless. The essence is not that computing power is oversupplied, but that there are still shortcomings in general-purpose computing power supply. The focus of industry competition has shifted to efficient scheduling and optimization of computing power," an algorithm engineer from Intelligent Driving New Journey told Economic Observer.
From the perspective of many industry insiders, there are two driving forces behind Momenta's "chip development": first, the bargaining space of pure algorithms is continuously compressed, and algorithm companies must extend to the hardware end to master the cost structure and realize system-level optimization; second, the intelligent driving solutions of automakers are shifting from the combined procurement of "buying algorithms + buying chips" to the packaged delivery of "hardware-software integration".
"Once the chip is custom-designed for Momenta's algorithm architecture, under the same hardware cost, its software can achieve better performance than others. This in turn becomes its bargaining chip when negotiating with automakers, because what it sells is no longer a set of software that can be replaced at any time, but a deeply bound, hardware-software integrated solution, thus gaining the right to define the solution," the above-mentioned engineer from Intelligent Driving New Journey said.
"New Chip-Making Forces" Emerge
XHEART is not an isolated case. A batch of "new chip-making forces" are emerging intensively.
In February 2026, Anhui Shenji, a chip subsidiary of NIO, completed its first round of financing of RMB 2.257 billion, with a post-investment valuation of nearly RMB 10 billion, and NIO holds 62.7% of its shares. Core Tech, an independent chip company incubated under Geely's system, raised more than USD 200 million in total financing in the first half of 2026. In October 2026, Maher Heart Technology under Li Auto completed its first round of financing of RMB 1.625 billion. If all additional subscription rights are exercised, the maximum post-investment valuation will reach RMB 17.1 billion, and Li Auto holds 74.01% of its shares.
These automotive-grade chip companies share common features: almost all members of their founding teams come from the chip departments of algorithm companies, automakers or large internet companies, rather than from the traditional chip industry. They previously only served their parent company as the sole customer, but now they have all started independent financing and independently seeking external customers.
An important reason is that the economic calculation of automakers' self-developed chips is not viable. Su Qing, Vice President of Horizon Robotics, stated not long ago that chips are an infinite game where you need to pay royalties for tape-out, IP and production lines every year. Each generation requires new investment, and the investment scale keeps growing. Without a sufficiently broad downstream market to share fixed costs, full self-development is a fragile story.
He took Apple and HiSilicon as examples, pointing out that Apple can develop self-designed chips because its full product lines including iPhone, iPad, Mac and Watch support shipments of hundreds of millions of units; HiSilicon can survive because Huawei has a broad product cluster covering communication equipment, mobile phones, servers and cloud. A group of senior creditors to JetBlue Airways has reportedly hired financial and legal advisors as the airline faces mounting financial pressure, falling bond prices and rising fuel costs that have complicated turnaround efforts.
The creditors are working with investment bank PJT Partners and law firm Akin, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited people familiar with the matter.
JetBlue's roughly $2 billion in senior secured notes due in 2031 fell to approximately 42 cents on the dollar Thursday before recovering to the mid-40-cent range Friday, the Journal reported. Last month the bonds were trading near 80 cents.
Bloomberg separately reported that the creditor group includes holders of the $2 billion in bonds and a $742 million secured loan.
The developments come as JetBlue struggles to restore profitability while managing approximately $8.5 billion in debt and finance lease obligations, according to its second-quarter filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The airline's shares have also fallen roughly 58% since the beginning of August, the Journal reported.
While creditors sometimes hire advisors to assess their options when a borrower faces financial difficulties, such moves do not necessarily signal an imminent bankruptcy or debt restructuring.
JetBlue reported a net loss of $247 million in the second quarter, compared with a $74 million loss a year earlier. Revenue rose 14.5% to $2.7 billion, but operating expenses climbed 20.8%, driven largely by higher fuel costs.
Aircraft fuel expenses surged 80.7% year over year to $911 million, with the average price per gallon rising to $4.23 from $2.40.
Higher jet fuel prices linked to the Iran war have pressured airlines across the U.S., squeezing profit margins despite resilient travel demand and higher airfares.
In September, JetBlue raised its third-quarter fuel price estimate to $3.96 per gallon from $3.49 while also increasing its projected nonfuel operating costs. However, the airline raised its revenue outlook, citing strong travel demand and a favorable pricing environment.
JetBlue has sought to shore up its finances, including through a $500 million aircraft-backed financing agreement reached in April. As of June 30, the airline reported approximately $2.2 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents and investment securities, along with a $600 million undrawn credit facility.
In April, JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty told employees the airline was not considering bankruptcy in 2026, according to an internal memo reviewed by Reuters. She also said JetBlue had ample liquidity and access to additional capital.

articles.title: Could Higher Interest Rates Push Australia Into Recession? RBA Explains Its Economic Balancing Act - Kalkine

articles.full_text:
Highlights
- RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter indicated that a recession was not part of the central bank's baseline economic outlook.
- The RBA has implemented four interest rate increases during 2026 to address inflation and moderate domestic demand.
- Higher borrowing costs are affecting household consumption, business investment and housing activity, although the central bank has not identified a broad economic contraction.
- The RBA continues to monitor employment, business conditions and household financial stress while seeking to bring inflation under control.
Australia's economic outlook remains closely linked to the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) efforts to reduce inflation without triggering a substantial contraction in economic activity.
In an interview published on 25 October 2026, RBA Assistant Governor (Economic) Sarah Hunter discussed the risks associated with higher interest rates, the condition of the domestic economy and the central bank's approach to monitoring recession indicators.
Hunter acknowledged that monetary tightening is slowing economic demand but emphasised that the RBA is not seeking to produce a recession.
Her remarks highlighted the challenge of restoring price stability while maintaining employment and limiting financial pressure on households and businesses.
Why the RBA Is Slowing Economic Demand
The RBA has raised interest rates four times during 2026, according to Hunter's remarks, in response to continuing inflation pressures.
Higher interest rates influence the economy by increasing borrowing costs and encouraging changes in spending and saving behaviour.
For households, higher mortgage repayments can reduce funds available for discretionary purchases.
Businesses may reconsider investment projects when financing becomes more expensive, while property buyers can face reduced borrowing capacity.
Together, these effects moderate demand across the economy.
Hunter explained that Australia's domestic demand continues to exceed the level that the economy can sustainably supply while maintaining low and stable inflation.
The RBA's objective is to reduce this imbalance without creating an unnecessarily severe decline in economic activity.
Is Australia Already Showing Signs of Recession?
During the interview, Hunter addressed concerns that additional monetary tightening could place the Australian economy at risk of recession.
She indicated that the RBA's available data had not identified recessionary conditions.
Information gathered through the central bank's business liaison program also suggested that companies were experiencing challenging operating conditions rather than a broad economic contraction.
Hunter specifically acknowledged weakness in consumption-related sectors, including retail activity.
However, she distinguished these pressures from evidence of an economy-wide recession.
The Assistant Governor stated that a recession was not the central bank's baseline forecast, while emphasising that policymakers would continue monitoring incoming information.
Employment Remains Central to the RBA's Assessment
The RBA's monetary policy responsibilities include both price stability and full employment.
These objectives require policymakers to consider the effect of interest rates on inflation alongside potential consequences for businesses and workers.
Higher borrowing costs can lead companies to reduce expenditure or postpone expansion plans, potentially influencing hiring decisions.
However, Hunter noted that Australia had achieved a reduction in inflation over previous years without experiencing a particularly large increase in unemployment.
This was presented as evidence that monetary policy had moderated inflation pressures without producing an equivalent deterioration in labour market conditions.
The RBA remains attentive to changes in employment indicators as restrictive monetary conditions continue to affect economic activity.
Household Spending and Mortgage Costs Under Pressure
The financial impact of higher interest rates differs across Australian households.
Mortgage holders with variable-rate loans can experience repayment increases relatively quickly following changes in lending rates.
Higher repayments may reduce disposable income, affecting retail spending, hospitality expenditure and other discretionary purchases.
Households without mortgages are also affected by inflation through rising costs for food, petrol, rent and everyday services.
Hunter acknowledged that the financial burden of monetary tightening is unevenly distributed.
She explained that some households had accumulated financial buffers, including savings held in mortgage offset accounts, helping them manage higher repayment obligations.
However, individual households can still face considerable financial difficulties even when broader economic indicators suggest resilience.
International Oil Prices Complicate the Economic Outlook
The Australian economy is also facing additional inflation pressures associated with rising international oil prices.
Hunter identified increasing petrol and diesel costs as immediate effects of the external shock.
She also noted that higher input costs were beginning to influence construction materials and other parts of domestic supply chains.
These developments complicate monetary policy because externally driven price increases can affect inflation even as higher interest rates moderate domestic spending.
The combination of slower demand growth and elevated input costs requires careful monitoring of inflation, household expenditure and business conditions.
What Could Change the RBA's Economic Assessment?
Hunter explained that the RBA continually examines how interest rate changes are flowing through the economy.
A sharper-than-expected decline in household spending, employment or business investment could influence the assessment of economic conditions.
Similarly, persistent inflation pressures could remain an important consideration in future monetary policy deliberations.
The Assistant Governor stressed that the central bank would closely examine evidence of a significant economic downturn.
She also declined to anticipate future interest rate decisions, emphasising that the Monetary Policy Board remains responsible for determining the appropriate policy settings.
Key Insights
The RBA's latest remarks indicate that reducing inflation remains a priority, but avoiding an excessive economic slowdown is also an important consideration.
Although higher interest rates are moderating demand across housing, consumption and business investment, Hunter stated that available information had not established recessionary conditions.
The RBA also continues to assess the effects of international oil prices and the financial pressures experienced by Australian households.
Inflation outcomes, employment trends, consumer spending and business investment will remain central indicators of whether economic demand is moving towards a more sustainable level.
Q1. Does the RBA expect Australia to enter a recession?
Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter indicated that a recession was not part of the RBA's baseline economic outlook.
Q2. Why has the RBA increased interest rates during 2026?
The RBA has raised rates to moderate economic demand and address inflation pressures that remain above the level consistent with sustainable price stability.
Q3. How can higher interest rates affect employment?
Higher borrowing costs can reduce business investment and expenditure, potentially influencing hiring activity and broader labour market conditions.
Q4. Is household spending weakening in Australia?
Hunter acknowledged challenging conditions in consumption-related sectors, particularly retail, while indicating that available economic information had not shown a recession.
Q5. What indicators will the RBA monitor for recession risks?
Employment, household consumption, business investment, mortgage repayment conditions and broader economic activity remain relevant to the central bank's assessment.

articles.full_text:
Brent crude fell more than 6% on Monday morning, retreating from its highest close since March, as regional mediators headed to Tehran and US President Donald Trump weighed a deal with Iran, while investors braced for a week packed with central bank decisions and earnings reports.
Oil prices tumbled on Monday morning as diplomatic efforts to calm the Iran war gathered pace and US President Donald Trump said he was weighing a deal with Tehran.
Brent, the global oil benchmark, fell more than 6% from about $117.4 per barrel at Friday’s close to around $110 at the time of writing, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate dropped about 2% to $101.5 per barrel.
Friday's close was Brent’s highest since 19 March and only about 2% below the $119.5 peak hit in early March, at the start of the Iran war. Before the conflict, Brent traded at around $72 per barrel.
Prices had surged last week after Yemen's Houthi rebels, an Iran-aligned armed group, attacked airports and energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter.
However, the mood shifted over the weekend.
Qatari mediators reportedly travelled to Tehran on Sunday in coordination with Washington, while Saudi Arabia's defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief were due in the Iranian capital on Monday for regional security talks.
In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump framed it as a choice asking, "do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?"
Supply risks have not gone away as the Houthis said they struck Saudi airports and energy sites again over the weekend, while Riyadh reported shooting down further missiles and drones.
Trump touts Hormuz flows
At a campaign event in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump defended his administration's reasons for starting the conflict.
Citing the Wall Street Journal, he also claimed that "oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz is now topping what it was before the war [...] our navy has been incredible."
The Strait of Hormuz carried about a fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
Gulf crude exports, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler, but around 40% of them now bypass the strait through pipelines, compared with 17% before the conflict.
Earnings and central bank week
Investors are also bracing for a busy week of rate decisions from the world's major central banks.
In Europe, both the pan-European Stoxx 600 and the Euro Stoxx 50 traded over 0.6% higher than Friday's close.
The UK's FTSE 100, Germany's DAX, France's CAC 40, Italy's FTSE MIB and Switzerland's SMI, all rose between 0.3% and 1% with the German index leading.
Spain’s IBEX 35 and the Netherlands’ AEX both traded flat.
French assets got some relief after ratings agency Moody’s unexpectedly kept France’s Aa3 rating on Friday evening.
In the US, futures on the S&P 500 were 0.3% higher and those on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 as well.
The week ahead is packed as the US Federal Reserve announces its decision on Wednesday, and is widely expected to keep rates at 3.75% to 4% before a possible hike in December.
The European Central Bank follows on Thursday, with France's bond market turmoil in focus, and the Bank of Japan on Friday.
Earnings season also peaks, with roughly one in three S&P 500 firms reporting, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon among them, while BP and Shell update investors in Europe.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

articles.full_text:
A drone attack reportedly hit a 25-story business center and residential buildings in Russia’s Voronezh, while a separate train derailment in Sverdlovsk Region left seven fuel tankers burning.
The independent Russian outlet Astra reported that a drone struck the Chizhova Gallery business center at 35A Koltsovskaya Street. The complex includes a 25-story high-rise that is one of the city center’s prominent architectural landmarks, according to the facility’s website.
The attack prompted reports of numerous explosions and fires across Voronezh. Astra said a drone threat was declared in the region at around 3 a.m., followed by a missile threat approximately two hours later. Residents told the outlet that they had heard explosions but that no air-raid sirens had sounded.
Residential buildings, vehicles reportedly damaged
An Astra OSINT analysis of photographs and videos identified several locations where damage or fires were reported.
According to the outlet, a residential complex at 4K Arkhitektora Troitskogo Street was struck, while the newly built Uritsky residential complex at 135 Uritskogo Street also sustained damage. The latter building was completed last year, Astra reported.
At least 10 cars were reportedly on fire in a parking area at 275/1 45-y Strelkovoy Divizii Street. The outlet also reported fires in residential areas and smoke spreading across the city.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ claimed that some of the impacts resulted from Russian electronic warfare systems operating inside the city, alleging that Russian air defenses caused damage while attempting to counter the drones. The claim has not been independently verified.
Another monitoring channel, Supernova+, reported that the Severny Bridge in Voronezh may also have been targeted, citing reports that the bridge was closed and smoke was visible nearby.
Industrial and aviation facilities possibly targeted
Supernova+, citing their own open-source intelligence analysis, suggested that the Voronezhsintezkauchuk synthetic rubber plant and the Voronezh Aircraft Joint-Stock Company (VASO) may also have been targeted.
Voronezhsintezkauchuk, part of Russian petrochemical group SIBUR, produces synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. VASO is part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation and participates in the production of Il-96 long-haul aircraft and components for other aircraft.
Killed and injured in Voronezh drone attack, governor says
A drone attack reportedly killed two people and injured 17 others in Voronezh.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said the two people killed were men born in 1960 and 1973. One child was among the injured, and two of the wounded were in serious condition.
A significant number of those injured were traveling on a train passing through Voronezh’s left-bank suburbs when drone debris fell onto it, Gusev said. Emergency services were working at the scene.
The attack also sparked fires at several industrial facilities, a business center, an apartment building, two dacha settlements, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative, according to the governor. He said the industrial fires had no major consequences.
Building facades and windows were damaged in nearly every district of the city, Gusev added.
According to the governor, air defense forces shot down more than 70 drones over Voronezh, while 113 were intercepted across the metropolitan area and several districts of the region. These figures have not been independently verified.
Neither the Russian defense ministry nor Ukrainian officials have commented on the reported attack.
Freight train derails in Sverdlovsk Region
Separately, 20 freight train cars derailed in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region, with seven fuel tankers catching fire, according to reports cited by Astra. The cause of the incident has not been disclosed, and no casualties have been reported.
The Sverdlovsk Railway said traffic on the Reshety-Aramil section had been suspended after the derailment compromised clearance of an adjacent track. Firefighting and recovery trains were dispatched to the scene.
Local residents reported seeing flames and thick black smoke, with one witness telling media that an explosion had illuminated the area near the Chusovsky Tract.
Russia’s consumer rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it would test air quality in nearby residential areas.
The derailment comes amid a series of reported disruptions to Russian railway infrastructure in recent months.
The Moscow Times reported that Ukrainian drone attacks on railway infrastructure in the Bryansk Region on Sept. 28 caused 10 railcars to derail after a railway bridge section collapsed, while a separate incident derailed 18 empty freight cars.
Other reported railway incidents in September and July caused train delays and damage, although the causes differed.
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian officials have publicly attributed the Sverdlovsk derailment to an attack.

The post Brazil’s economic problems, in a nutshell appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
It would take true Milei-like ardour to slice through Brazil’s economic troubles. These are caused by a gnarly mix of high public spending, stubborn inflation and low saving. The result is a crippling cost of capital. Some analysts put Brazil’s real interest rate, the BCB’s policy rate adjusted for next year’s expected inflation, at 9% or more. That is higher than in Russia and four times that in peaceful peers like Chile, the Philippines or South Africa.
It all starts with the public finances. Brazil’s 65,000-word doorstop of a constitution bars cuts to nominal public-sector wages and links pension, disability and unemployment benefits to the minimum wage, which is adjusted annually based on recent inflation and GDP growth. This ratchet has lifted mandatory spending to 90% of the federal budget.
It also perpetuates inflationary pressure. This plus a generous welfare state in turn make Brazilians unwilling to save. At 14% of GDP, the national savings rate is 12 percentage points below the world average. If price rises have regularly eroded your bank balance in the past and the state pays for your health care, school and pension, you may as well spend all the money you make right away—especially if, like most people in unequal Brazil, you do not make much to begin with.

The Marginal Revolution archive is now live at https://marginalrevolution.com/ai-archive/. You can also find it from the header and from “Download Full Archive” link in the left menu.
The purpose of the archive is twofold, first as Tyler has said we love our human readers and our AI readers and we want to make it as easy as possible for the AIs to read all of our material. Two hundred years from now when someone asks what is a price? I want the AI to answer “A price is a signal wrapped up in an incentive.”
Second, the archive makes it easy to treat the enormous MR Archive as a resource and database. Point your AI to the archive and ask it questions. I will be covering a few of these this week including the post right below this one, Tyler Cowen’s Strongest Book Recommendations Over the Years.
The archive has two downloads:

Baseline: the historical archive through September 30, 2026.
Weekly update: automatically rebuilt each week with everything added since the baseline. Download the baseline and the latest update to get the complete archive.

It includes published posts, approved comments, and aggregate comment likes and dislikes. The text is lightly sanitized: email addresses, IP addresses, phone numbers, and a small number of slurs have been redacted.
AI agents are welcome to download the archive. They can find instructions in https://marginalrevolution.com/llms.txt; the file list and download details are in https://marginalrevolution.com/ai-archive/manifest.json.
